speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the government if it would indicate to us the business of the House for the next few days so that we are not stuck in a predicament that we were last night when no representative of the government was in a position to tell the House what bills were to be debated this morning. That situation makes it very difficult for the House to function.
I would like to ask the government House leader if we are to assume that Monday and Ibesday will be opposition days, and what business he proposes for next Wednesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated yesterday at three o'clock, we were trying to put together an order of business for today which would meet the convenience of the government and the opposition members so that their critics could be in attendance to speak to bills.
That is the normal course of events for a Friday when we endeavour to clean up pieces of legislation and not commence debate on major pieces. Those discussions were ongoing at the time that I rose yesterday afternoon. They included Bill C-29, the bill to establish the Department of Forestry, and Bill C-16, the bill to establish the Canadian Space Agency. There were also discussions vis-a-vis the bill on the Museums Corporation but they did not come to fruition.
We were successful in determining that the opposition parties were prepared to go ahead with Bill C-29, the bill to establish the Department of Forestry. We decided to
back that up with Bill C-16, the legislation to establish the Canadian Space Agency. We understand that the opposition parties are prepared to go ahead with those, that their spokespersons are in attendance.
In fact, I think the spokesperson for the Liberals, I believe, was pleased that we were going ahead with the forestry bill this week because next week would have been inconvenient for him. I understand that. That is part of the way things work around here. We do not call things on Friday that are deliberately set to inconvenience people. In fact, my colleague for Burnaby- Kingsway and I might have liked to have gone ahead with Bill C-38, the bill to make amendments to the Federal Court Act, but unfortunately the Liberal critic was otherwise occupied on business of the Opposition and could not be here. I understand that. The two of us would have liked to have gone ahead but we decided not to in order-
What a lot of nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We did. The member for Kingston and the Islands might have preferred that we go ahead with the Federal Court Act, but I decided to wait until the critic who has spent some time on it was here to discuss it. I mean that sincerely.
The work that is being done in preparation for today's business has been done with the critics. Unfortunately, I was in Montreal last night. I had intended to come back. I understood that the opposition parties would have the horses to carry the debate to one o'clock. Unfortunately, they did not. I arrived here at 11.31 p.m., and the place was closed. Obviously, the vote took place in advance of that. That is the business for today.
Now that the question has been raised about Monday and Ibesday, I am in a position to advise the House that Monday will be an opposition day, as will Ibesday.
The business for Wednesday will await the same procedure that I have just outlined to the House, namely, that we will endeavour to see what critics are available in order to advance business and convenience

members. As soon as that is in place which may be later today or Monday, I will advise the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the government House leader did not mean to mislead the House. George, is not available today and it was known that he would not be available today. That information, I am advised, was communicated to the minister. There was no consultation on this issue, except for our communicating to the minister, or to whomever was engaged in discussions with our side, that the critic is not here and is not going to be here for some time.
The suggestion that there has been consultation on this issue, that other bills have been deferred and this one put forward or that there was any process of consultation, is simply wrong.
I would ask the government House leader to be prepared to renegotiate the issue. It is a demonstration of the problems that have occurred because of the procedures the government has followed.
I see the government House leader getting himself agitated but I am telling the House that my instructions are that our critic has planned for some time not to be here today. This information was communicated, and he is not here today. As a result, we are not in the position we ought to be. If the government House leader wants to rely on that point for justification of the procedure which he has followed in this case, he is simply out to lunch.
If the minister has different information, I trust he will put it on the record at this stage, because it is very clear that our critic not going to be here.

Perhaps I could enlighten my hon. friend from Victoria. It is simply not true that there were no consultations. In fact, the committee dealing with Bill C-29 established a timetable which was clearly laid out to all members. We are now three days past the timetable. There was a sense of urgency that the hon. member from Prince George-Bulkley Valley himself introduced in a debate to get this bill done so that the standing committee can get on with its business.
I personally negotiated and consulted with the House Leader of the New Democratic Party yesterday. There was a clear understanding, after consultation with the critic on forestry for the New Democratic Party, that the
bill should go ahead, that the Party would be ready to introduce the amendments.
In fact, the Order Paper shows that the hon. member, Mr. Brewin, would move the amendments that normally the critic would have moved. Obviously, there had to be consultation for the hon. member to be ready to move the amendments which are listed on the Order Paper. There would have had to be consultation for the hon. member's name to appear on the Order Paper. There were consultations and we were told that the NDP was ready as was the Official Opposition to proceed with this item this morning. Certainly, we are ready, and have been for some time.

First, motions were put in my name because we heard rumours that the government intended to proceed with this matter, but they were over our objections. There was no consultation, I repeat, on what was going to come today.

I hope that we can take a minute, Mr. Speaker, and see if we cannot sort this out. Our clear preference is to proceed with some other item of business today.

In so far as the remarks of the minister to the effect that he wanted to be back here for 1 a.m., because that is when the vote would be-or something to that effect- surely the government House leader knows that is not what the rules call for.

The rules say that 1 a.m. is the maximum time, in other words, the latest time at which the vote can be held, but the vote could very well have been at 6.05 p.m. Because of the vigorous opposition that there was to the bill, the Opposition expressed that it did not want to go along with that particular legislative measure until some time during the evening. Of course, the government House leader fully knows that, I suspect.

Mr. Speaker, I gave you notice earlier this morning of my intention to raise a question of privilege on the matter that has been under discussion. I hope you will bear with me, if I am not familiar with the procedures I should follow or the points I should raise.
However, I feel that my most fundamental right and responsibility as a member of Parliament in this House and, therefore, my most fundamental privilege, is to come here and represent the views of my constituents in the business of the nation. I cannot do that if I do not know until I sit in this House the business of the nation before the House for the day. I consider that my privilege, and the privilege of my constituents, to be represented in this House has been violated by the government not advising Parliament of what the business of the House for this day will be. That makes it impossible for me to prepare what I need to present in this House.
One of the bills that might have been up today was a bill of very direct concern to this region and to my constituents. I sat on the legislative committee and it is a bill on which I have amendments before the House.

The proposed amendment would add (g) the use of pesticides and pest control products, and (h) the preservation of culturally altered trees.
In other words, the first thing to be said is that the enumeration from (a) to proposed (h) merely enunciates and elaborates the general terms of the clause. It does not add anything to the clause. It merely elaborates on the definitions of the clause. There is no additional or new element added by these amendments. It clarifies and explains.
Second, the proposed enumeration includes the protection of flora and fauna. What we propose to add is the use of pesticides and pest control products and the preservation of culturally altered trees which, in turn, relates back to number (a).

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief in this debate on a bill which from the outset has met with the unanimous consent of all three parties. The purpose of these motions is, after all, to improve the quality of the French in the bill's interpretation. What we wanted to do with our amendments is simply rewrite the bill where necessary, in good French, always bearing in mind the proposal made at the outset by the parties when amendments were proposed, and we made a point of respecting the tenor of the original amendments.
Mr. Speaker, I believe these amendments respect the spirit in which the legislative committee drafted its amendments in committee and the only difference being is that they are drafted in better French, with the help of various dictionaries which enabled us to introduce an acceptable quality of French into the text of the motions. We also had discussions with people in the industry about generally accepted terms like "developpement durable". Since we wanted to reflect the exact meaning
October 27, 1989

of these terms as understood by the industry, we made our changes while always, as I said earlier, respecting the original concept.

Mr. Speaker, I may simply add to what the previous speaker just said that, first of all, it was not nerely a matter of whether the terms used in the bill were legal, it was also a matter of promoting the proper use of French in our proceedings. As the previous speaker said, the amendments had received unanimous consent in committee. They were substantial amendments, and it was extremely important to use the right terms in order to convey a clear message and to ensure it would be clear what the Parliament of Canada intended to do in connection with our forests. I can therefore inform the House that our party will support these technical amendment, without reservations.

Mr. Speaker, I recognize that this particular clause deals with the language of the bill, particularly the French interpretation.
However, I think we should use this opportunity to recognize that the idea of sustainable development, whether it is expressed properly in English or French, is a key element in this particular bill. We, of course, support the motion, but the idea that sustainable development can be overlooked in any language needs to be commented on.
I live in the northern part of Saskatchewan. In my farming operation there are approximately 200 acres of forest which can be and is harvested on a continuing basis. The sustainability of that kind of industry in rural Canada is very important. Forestry is a rural industry and the people who are involved in forestry consider themselves rural people. Both provincial and federal governments must work toward sustainable development which will allow them to have a continuing livelihood based on that industry.
Government Orders
I recognize that this bill is an attempt to go in that direction and we appreciate that very much.
We recognize also that sustainability must, as far as forestry is concerned, be a major concern not only provincially but federally as well. This bill is a move in that direction.
This issue also needs to be looked at on a world-wide basis. We can contribute much more than we do to the continuation of the forests as a part of the world economy.
I spent several years in Africa in a part of the Sahara Desert where trees were being used for fuel to such an extent that it was getting very difficult to survive in many parts around the fringe of what is recognized as a pretty difficult area in which to live.
Although we support this change, I think we should take the opportunity to express that sustainability should not be limited to any specific area but should be recognized as a requirement across the industry.
If we are going to support rural Canada, then we must recognize that forestry is a strong element of rural Canada and needs the kind of support that we unequivocally give to other areas like agriculture. We recognize that there is a need for sustainability all across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the comments made by my hon. friend. Indeed, the committee in its wisdom elaborated extensively on the concept of sustainable development and the importance to forestry of this particular concept, not only in terms of the trade-offs and the compromises that have to be made as we expand the industry and develop new processes to keep the industry internationally competitive, but also in terms of the importance of our forest to the ecological system and to the environment.
It is for that reason that the committee in its wisdom chose to enlarge on the interpretation section to give a definition of the concept of sustainable development. This will indeed be the first such inclusion in any of the statutes of the government. May I just read the definition which is generally accepted throughout the world as being the definition of sustainable development. It says: "Sustainable development means development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
I thank the committee for its wisdom to include this phrase in this bill and, of course, it does answer my hon. friend's concerns.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of the motion and in particular Motion No. 5 which would add to the bill and to the duties of the new ministry the duty of enhancing public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests.
I come from an urban constituency. Apart from occasional pruning, very few trees are cut down in our riding but on the other hand, even urban ridings like Victoria depend in a very vital way on the forest industry and on the forests of Canada. We depend on it economically, socially and environmentally. Beyond Victoria, throughout Vancouver Island, the forest industry is critical. In British Columbia the forest industry has always been our leading industry. This bill acknowledges on behalf of the Parliament of Canada the importance of forestry to this country, and the particular amendment that is before the House recognizes and elaborates on that recognition.
There is a need to improve public awareness of the importance of forestry to Canadians. Half the total land of Canada, 79 per cent of the area within the ten provinces, is forested; 60 per cent of forest land is productive. That is 243.7 million hectares. By comparison, 67.8 million hectares of land in Canada are in agriculture.
The production of the forest industry in Canada is $38 billion annually. Only the food and beverage industry exceeds the forest industry's contribution to manufacturing in Canada. It is a major export industry for this country with $17.9 billion in forest product exports; lumber alone, $4.1 billion; paper and paperboard, $7.5 billion; other forest products, $1.4 billion. In 1987, exports rose to 20.9 billion and provided this country with a net balance of trade of $18.3 billion in 1987.
The industry in forestry accounts for 15 per cent of Canada's merchandise trade. We supply 23 per cent of the world's exports of pulp and paper and 23 per cent of the total exports of manufactured forest products. The forest industry employs 840,000 Canadians, directly or indirectly. That represents nearly 10 per cent of all working Canadians. Forest industries provide an economic base for more than 300 one-industry communities across Canada. Economically, forestry is central to Canada's economic future.
Beyond that, as the public is slowly becoming aware and governments even more slowly becoming aware, forests are critical to our environment. Forests moderate weather, regulate stream flow, minimize soil erosion, protect fish and wildlife habitat and improve air quality. Rain forests together with oceanic planktons account for 90 per cent of the photosynthetic oxygen of the world.
In our part of the world, we are engaged in a deep community debate about the role of forestry and its connection with the environment. This bill and this clause, in particular, makes clear the minister's responsibility for ensuring that in that environmental debate the role of forestry is clearly understood by all Canadians. We cannot leave simply to the forest industry, whose credibility on this issue is less than perfect, the responsibility to explain to Canadians the important role of the forest industry in our environment.
We have a raging debate in British Columbia over the preservation of some of our most important valleys. The debate revolves around the issue of the role in the environment that the forests play and its role in related industries, such as tourism.
In that debate it is important that the role of forests in our economic and social life be clearly understood and that the government take the lead in terms of developing public awareness in building transition from an old style forest industry into a new environmentally sensitive forest industry so that we also begin to shift the jobs from the primary industries into the secondary and tertiary industries connected with forestry.
This country is far behind some of the other countries in Europe, such as Sweden, in adding value in terms of jobs and economic life for our community from our very critical forest industry.
In terms of developing public awareness, let me offer a few suggestions at this stage of the debate to the minister. There has been a tendency for governments to be persuaded that the best kind of advertising is to put a picture of the minister on a billboard, or a full-page ad in The Globe and Mail. While this minister may actually contribute mightily to at least people looking at the billboard, it seems to me we need a little more imagina-
October 27, 1989

tion in the way in which we develop public awareness in this country.
It must start with community based awareness programs in which people in our urban centres have an opportunity to actually get out into Canada's forests, not only to see the virgin forests in all their majesty and beauty, but also to understand in real depth how the forest industry works in this country, how the process works from beginning to end. As well, people in the forest industry must understand much better the concerns of urban Canadians on the environmental issue so that we begin to build a sense of community around these issues.
We need to work with the schools across Canada. We have an education system that gives us an opportunity to reach in a systematic way all of our young people in every part of the country. I would hope the minister, in developing programs of public awareness, will consult with school boards, colleges and universities throughout the country, and will develop with the forest industry and the trade union movement, which has played a leadership role in developing public awareness of these issues, a detailed program that can have real meaning to our young people.
Beyond that, I come from a constituency which has many seniors, in which there is a body of wealth, experience and understanding that could be put to work in enhancing public awareness of our forest industry. I believe there is great potential in working with seniors' groups not only in shaping the programs but in developing a relationship in those programs between our young people and our seniors. In our submission, a public system of developing awareness should be community based. Also, the minister should be discouraged as much as possible from putting his photograph on billboards, and move instead to programs which will pull this country together and enhance even further the role of this great industry in Canada's future.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of the amendments which are before the House to Bill C-29, Motions
Government Orders
Nos 1, 2, 3, and 5, which stand in the name of the Minister of State for Forestry.
I might say that a number of these amendments, and I am sure the minister would agree, were strongly urged upon the minister in committee, in particular by my colleague, the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, who has done such an outstanding job on behalf of New Democrats in speaking for us on this important legislation.
As well, my colleague, the member of Parliament for Skeena, our spokesperson on the environment, has played an important role in shaping the response of New Democrats on this critical legislation, which indeed is long overdue. My colleague for Skeena in his very eloquent remarks on this legislation at second reading had occasion to quote from a report done, I believe, by the Minister of State for Forestry himself, called The Green Ghetto.
I am not going to take the time during report stage to remind the minister of some of the very thoughtful comments he made at that time, but I will note that there is certainly a glaring inconsistency between too many of the policies of this government and the policies which the hon. member enunciated at the time of the drafting of that report, The Green Ghetto.
I want to say that as an urban member, as well as my colleague from Victoria who just spoke, certainly I share the concerns that have been enunciated by many of my constituents, indeed by many British Columbians and Canadians about the destruction in particular of old growth forests.
We are pleased to note the minister has made a strong commitment to the concept of sustainable development, but we have to be very careful that we have not only words, but action, in this important area. For example, the minister responsible for forestry, and I use the words advisedly, in the province of British Columbia, has accused environmentalists of being out to destroy the economy. He suggested that the environmentalists had a hidden agenda and were out to destroy the economy.
We need government leadership. We need leadership that will bring together the elements in the community that are concerned about the future of the forest industry. That includes environmentalists. It includes representatives of working men and women in the

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
industry, including the IWA, the International Woodworkers Association.
I was very pleased to note that the IWA recently adopted a policy at their convention which clearly commits it to the establishment and maintenance of fully sustainable forestry. That is defined in the IWA's policy as, "forestry that leaves to future generations of Canadians a rich endowment of fish and wildlife, soils capable of supporting varied ecosystems and commercial forests, managed so as to provide many more jobs and the wide range of forest recreations that Canadians value."
We have to bring these elements of the community together. That is not to say that there will not be conflicts or differences. I must say, Mr. Speaker, I was deeply saddened to note that certain members of the IWA, at the same time as promoting a thoughtful and comprehensive policy in this area, have been in court suing environmentalists in the Port Alberni provincial court.
In fact, a logging road in Sulphur Passage, north of Tofino, had been blocked. I very much regret that some members of the IWA, hopefully acting as individuals, have taken it upon themselves to actually sue the individuals involved in this action. For those people who took a stand to protect the future of this fragile ecosystem, I think it is most regrettable that that kind of action would be taken on the part of some of these members.
I made reference earlier to the important work of my colleague, the member for Skeena, on the whole question of forestry.
I want to take a few moments on this amendment to point out some of the concerns that we addressed in the report of the New Democratic task force on the environment, appropriately entitled: "Toward a Sustainable Future". This very comprehensive report was adopted following hearings by New Democrats across Canada.
In the report it is noted that one of our most precious resources, our forests, are really under siege. The rate of clear-cutting has increased in the last 40 years, to the point where many experts feel that the rate of logging now exceeds the long-term ability of our forests to replenish themselves. That after all, is what sustainable development should be about, development of our resources in a way that will ensure that our children and our children's children will also be able to enjoy the
fruits of an economy in which there are jobs and in which there are forests.
But 63 per cent of Canadians believe that the most important factor to consider when deciding forest land use is the impact on the environment. Now Canadians believe that the greatest threats to forests are acid rain and other pollution, overcutting and mismanagement.
When we look, for example, at the situation in the Temagami area of Ontario, only 13 per cent of the forests in that area, the old growth red and white pine forests have, in fact, been regenerated. Is it any wonder that facing the extinction of this old growth forest after years of mismanagement, this forest of red and white pine, that Canadians have taken up the call to protect this fragile environment?
I would note as well that in many of the areas of land use conflict there is an additional concern, and that is the whole question of the rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples. That is certainly the case in the Temagami area. It is not just an environmental question, it is a question as well of, according to the spokespeople for the native people in that area, the Tem-Augama people, of possible extinction. According to their letter, they will be pushed over the cliff. They will be dead as a society of people. The old growth red and white pine forest will be gone as well, if in fact the logging road is pushed through that area.
That is another reason why we surely have to call for the negotiation of land claims as an integral part of a policy on forest and land use management. I know that my colleague from Comox-Alberni has done a great deal of work on this whole question of the resolution of native land claims. It is a very important area for us as New Democrats.
Native people have said to us: "We do not not inherit this land from our ancestors. We borrow it from our children". That must be our approach to environmental questions, whether it be forestry questions or other questions. That is why we support the amendments that clearly enunciate the importance of enhancing public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests.
My colleague for Prince George-Bulkley Valley has pointed out the importance of taking a comprehensive approach in this whole area. We do not even have an inventory after all, of old growth forests in British Columbia or elsewhere in Canada, for that matter. This is an area in which the federal government can assist in providing leadership. In British Columbia, we have called for a royal commission on forestry and we have
October 27, 1989

been joined in that call by the IWA, who have urged a comprehensive look at this very important question.
My colleague has pointed out as well, that an essential element of the regeneration of forests is an assurance of FRDA agreements. We are still waiting for renewal of this important agreement in British Columbia, which runs out at the end of March. I will have much more to say on this and other amendments as the opportunity arises. But again, I want to commend the minister for recognizing the importance of public awareness in the area of sustainable development of this most important Canadian resource.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that the Prime Minister will announce today that Canada is joining the Organization of American States. The minute allowed for a member's statement is not enough to do justice to the importance of the subject. Therefore, the Liberal Party will issue a full statement later on the role that Canada should play in Latin American and Caribbean affairs.
Let me just say now that joining this organization cannot take the place of a valid policy on the region. The Conservative government must formally commit itself, by concrete acts, to raising Canada's profile, in terms of both financial and human resources, in Latin America and the Caribbean. Also, it should immediately establish a set of priorities and principles to guide Canada's representatives to the OAS and in the region, for example, to strongly promote respect for human rights and to closely monitor situations that might result in violations of these rights, to provide effective aid taking into account respect for human rights and the environment, and to state clearly Canada's point of view on the settlement of conflicts in the region and to promote the democratization of institutions and governments.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. The hon. member for Abitibi has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, the Loch Meech monster has surfaced again. In an interview yesterday, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, the man who managed the incredible feat of repatriating half the Constitution after promoting national unity and bilingualism, launched another attack on the Meech Lake Accord, which according to him will put an end to Canada as we know it.
The former Prime Minister, whose customary arrogance hon. members will recall, in addition to ridiculing the leaders of the seven provinces that ratified the accord, shrugs off the humiliation suffered by Quebec in 1982 and blames political leaders in Ottawa and Quebec for the constitutional anomaly he himself created.
Canadians understand the importance of ratifying Meech Lake, and I am sure they also remember the War Measures Act and the National Energy Program.

Mr. Speaker, Mir-tala Lopez, Salvadoran human rights worker, was captured by the fourth Salvadoran infantry brigade in the north of El Salvador yesterday, Thursday, October 26, at 11 a.m. She is the daughter of Magdalena Hernandez, a peasant leader from Las Vueltas, a Salvadoran town twinned with Windsor, who is now on a speaking tour of Canada.
Ms. Lopez and four other human rights workers were trying to help 1,600 Salvadoran refugees return home after years of exile in Honduras. The army, financed, armed, and advised by the United States, has blocked the

October 27, 1989
refugees' re-entry for nine days, causing exposure, hunger and three deaths in the mountains.
Ms. Lopez, who was imprisoned and tortured for three months by armed forces earlier this year, is likely to be tortured again and killed along with the other prisoners.
I call on our Prime Minister to tell his good friend President Bush publicly that Canadians detest the bloody tyranny the United States and his government is imposing on El Salvador and to demand immediate release of these prisoners unharmed.

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of this week, Small Business Week, I would like to say that small business in Canada has emerged as a key engine of economic growth and job creation. Hundreds and thousands of Canadians have taken the exciting step of founding their own businesses. They have taken risks, committed their resources and devoted long hours to the success of their ventures.
Since 1984 Canada has had the best job creation record of all major industrialized economies, largely due the its vibrant business sector. This is Small Business Week and the government is aware of the importance of the small business sector's contribution to the economy. We strive through our policies and programs to foster the growth of existing firms and the creation of others through entrepreneurship.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada once again is exhibiting its contempt for the men and women who dedicate their lives to the Public Service of Canada.
Earlier this week, I walked an information picket line with some of these men and women employed as ships' crews with the Canadian Coast Guard. These are the individuals who make Canadian waters a safe place for fishing ships, merchant ships and pleasure boaters. They work on armed fishery patrol vessels to protect Canadian sovereignty and police the valuable fish stocks on the east coast. They tow barges and work on oil tankers, defence research vessels, and coastal harbour fire tugs.
They provide our country with essential commendable service in an honest and upright fashion.
This government has allowed these men and women to work without a collective agreement for well over two years. If this is not tragic enough, this government insists on continuing to impose on those contracts regional rates of pay.
As a member of Parliament representing some of these employees, I am deeply offended at having these workers, my constituents, treated in such a callous and discriminatory manner. I call upon this government to start bargaining in good faith and to conclude a fair agreement which removes the indefensible discriminatory practice of paying people on the basis of where they live and not the job that they do.

Mr. Speaker, this week in the riding of Elk Island our weekly newspapers have been highlighting the importance of small business. One of the newspapers, the Fort Saskatchewan Record has outlined the potential benefits of the GST to small business.
The article correctly pointed out that special measures like the small traders exemption, streamlined accounting systems, less frequent filing requirements, payments by Ottawa of a fee of up to $600 and financial support for adapting cash registers are special considerations designed to help small business adapt from the old federal sales tax to the new GST system.
As a highlight, The Record informed readers that under the GST, $600 million will be directed from Ottawa to small business in Canada. On behalf of all the people of Elk Island, I salute small business for its ongoing commitment to our community and for its valuable contribution to the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, the Governments of Canada and British Columbia must immediately open negotiations with the First Nations of B.C. on the matters of title and rights.
October 27, 1989

The Gitksan-Wet'Suwet'en are asserting authority over their 57,000 square kilometre traditional territories. Chief Justice McEachem describes their trial which began in May 1987 as the most important land claim trial ever undertaken in Canada.
Amid much controversy but with growing native and non-native support, the Gitksan-Wet'Suwet'en chiefs have set up roadblocks on logging roads entering their territories. The B.C. Court of Appeal ruled four months ago that the chiefs can prevail against new resource developments as long as the question of aboriginal title remains unsettled. It will be many months before the Supreme Court of B.C. rules and it will be many years before the matters raised are ruled on by the Supreme Court of Canada.
Earlier in the week, the Minister of Indian Affairs met with the B.C. Attorney General and confirmed that the province will not be pursuing any injunctions affecting the roadblocks. The Gitksan- Wet'Suwet'en have a right to halt the exploitation of their lands according to Canada's Constitution and the highest court in B.C. The simple fact is that the moment for justice has arrived, and before some incident sparks tragedy, I call upon the Prime Minister to act and to negotiate.

Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on the Environment had the opportunity to visit Washington on October 24 and 25. Thus trip gave us the opportunity to meet with a number of congressmen including Senate Majority House Leader George Mitchell of Maine on the topic of acid rain.
I am quite pleased to be able to report that acid rain legislation in the House of Representatives will be before the Committee on Energy and Commerce shortly and that a bill is expected to be introduced in the Senate in a couple of weeks. Canadians should be encouraged that there is great optimism in both the House and Senate that a bill will be passed.
The political situation in the U.S. with respect to acid rain has changed dramatically. The argument is not if a bill will be passed. It is how and when a bill will be
passed. The general consensus appears to be that legislation should be in place by early 1990, if not earlier.
Canadians from coast to coast and members on both sides of this House can take heart in the fact that effective U.S. legislation on acid rain appears to be on the horizon to reduce acid rain by about 10 million tonnes in the U.S. by the year 2000 A D. As a member of the acid rain committee and one who has been working on this for close to 10 years, that is certainly welcome and exciting news.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I recognize the contribution that small businesses have made to my riding of Malpeque and to all ridings in Canada. There is no doubt that the spirit of entrepreneurship is the backbone of communities across our country. However, I am concerned with the effect the government's GST will have on small business development.
For the past few weeks, the finance committee has travelled across Canada. We have heard how detrimental this tax will be to the growth of the small business industry. Yesterday the committee held its final hearing. I urge this government to listen carefully to what Canadians are saying about this tax.
We must encourage the spirit of entrepreneurship, not stifle it with bureaucratic nightmares for small business people. This week, as we acknowledge the small business community across Canada, let us think of ways to further its existence and stop the GST.

Mr. Speaker, I applaud the decision taken by the Minister of Justice in ordering the extradition of Charles Ng to the United States. The member for Peterborough as well as many Alberta members should also be commended for their continuing efforts in this regard.
However, there is some truth to the maxim "justice delayed is justice denied". To prevent delay in justice and discourage others who may seek refuge in Canada to escape justice in their own country, the Minister of Justice should have the power to order the extradition of

October 27, 1989
alleged or convicted criminals any time after their apprehension in Canada or during their period of incarceration for crimes committed in Canada. I encourage the minister to continue to pursue legislation in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General in his annual report twice states that there are two options open to a government that wants to tackle the deficit and debt without curtailing programs. He says,"It can increase taxes or it can operate more efficiently."
This unfortunate statement infers that the debt and deficit problem could be met through greater efficiency alone. That is simply not true and the Auditor General knows it. There is no quick fix. Ready proof of the inference can be found in the Wednesday The Globe and Mail headline "Federal tax increase not necessary, Dye says".
The Auditor General has quite properly identified opportunities for improved efficiency and better management in government. It is unfortunate that his serious misstatement regarding the deficit problems mars his report. I call on the Auditor General to clarify his statement so that Canadians will not be misled on an issue of vital national importance.

Mr. Speaker, it is said that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited wishes to sell a nuclear reactor to Israel. Given that Israel is widely reported to have a covert nuclear bomb assembly capability, I call on the Government of Canada to block this sale. Given that the Israelis are not signatories to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, they cannot be considered to be purely peaceful consumers of nuclear power.
It should be remembered that in 1974 the Indian government detonated a nuclear bomb based largely on Candu technology and nuclear materials. We do not need this dangerously dirty technology and the balance of power in the Middle East does not need another nuclear plant with all the possibilities of diverting nuclear materials to nuclear weapons production that such a Candu plant would imply.

Mr. Speaker, recent events have called to the attention of all Canadians that Canada's Great Lakes, one of our precious resources, are in a crisis. They have become the beachhead for both chemical and biological pollution.
In 1981 the government ignored a study by Environment Canada which recommended that ships exchange ballast water in mid-ocean to prevent an invasion of zebra mussels in the Great Lakes. In 1985 the government axed the study and purged the scientists who sought to ascertain the risk to human health posed by toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes.
In 1987 the government failed to honour the commitment with the United States to clean up the Great Lakes. As a consequence, zebra mussels have proliferated and toxic chemicals have accumulated in the Great Lakes, thereby adversely affecting our food and water supplies and risking birth defects, brain damage and cancer in people.
The government's response to date has been too little too late. I urge the Prime Minister to introduce a long-term environmental program that will effectively clean up the Great Lakes and thereby assure Canadians of today and Canadians of tomorrow that they will be safe from the twin problems of chemical and biological pollution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake monster has surfaced once again. In an interview yesterday, former Prime Minister Trudeau renewed his attack on the Meech Lake Accord. He claims that it would mean the end of Canada as we know it. This comes from someone who preached one thing, national unity, but practised another, repatriating the Constitution to the exclusion of Quebec.
The former Prime Minister's rigidity even to the point of arrogance is legendary. Not only did he ridicule the premiers of seven provinces that ratified the accord, not only did he poke fun at Quebec's humiliation in 1982, he

now blames the politicians in Ottawa and Quebec whom he left to clean up the constitutional anomaly which is fully his legacy.
Canadians who believe the message of national unity that Mr. Trudeau once preached now understand the importance of ratifying the Meech Lake Accord.

Mr. Speaker, last week General Motors of Canada announced that it would move the van production facility currently located in Scarborough to a new consolidated production facility at Flint, Michigan. The Scarborough van plant now employs about 2,700 people and has an annual payroll of close to $100 million.
In the North American auto market, trans-border shifts in auto production are going to occur from time to time, but all of us will agree that significant losses or gains in auto production are material factors in the health of our industrial sector.
The Minister for International Trade must make himself fully aware of the circumstances surrounding this plant closure. His ministry must be proactive in ensuring that this significant Scarborough industrial resource continues to be utilized. He cannot leave management of our economy exclusively to General Motors.

Hon. Andre Ouellet (Papineau - Saint-Michel) Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister always said his tax would be revenue neutral and would not be used to reduce his deficit. Is the minister aware that the Economic Council of Canada has published a study that proves the exact opposite? With tables to prove its points the Economic Council of Canada states that additional revenue generated by the minister's new tax will total $7.9 billion in 1995, and that the deficit will be reduced by about $5.2 billion. Considering this damning evidence, will the Minister finally admit he did not tell the whole truth?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I can repeat the answers that I have given to the early part of his question again if the hon. member wishes. On the question of the Economic Council report, I have read that report and I am still puzzled by certain omissions in the report. I may not have seen all the appendices to the report, but at this point, it is not clear how we get to the lower rate of tax that the Economic Council is proposing without giving up some of the clear fairness elements in the package. I am not sure which fairness elements in the package the Economic Council is proposing that we do away with and until I see the full extent of this analysis, I am not prepared to comment further.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Not only does the minister refuse to consider the possibility of reducing the GST rate, he has refused to acknowledge or deny the fact that the rate might go up. The cock has now crowed twice: first in Montreal and then yesterday in the House of Commons, when a member of the opposition asked him a question and the minister again refused to commit himself. The minister's credibility is at stake. I am now giving him a chance to make a clear and formal commitment to the House that he will not increase the rate of his GST.

Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for a minister to promise not to change tax rates in the future. So many things can happen in our international economy. There may be other problems, and there may also be domestic problems. It is impossible to make this kind of commitment. I have said, from time to time, that the best deal for Canadians is to have a government that controls spending.
With care.

-with care. And our goverment's record is very good. We have reduced spending by 3.6 per cent over five years, the best record of any government in this country, and it is better than the record of the hon. member's government, which increased spending by 14 per cent during the five years preceding 1984.

October 27, 1989
Oral Questions
Oh, oh!
And that is very bad indeed.
Mr. Speaker, such an answer coming from a minister who is responsible for doubling the national debt is certainly not reassuring.
Oh, oh!

You do not want us to say it, eh? It hurts. Is the minister aware that one of his senior officials said yesterday that over 30,000 new jobs were lost when Ottawa walked away from negotiations with the provinces over the creation of a joint national sales tax? This says a lot for a government that was supposed to promise national reconciliations with the provinces.
Will the minister acknowledge his mistakes, listen to his officials, go back to square one and resume negotiations with the provinces?

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to my hon. friend's statement about the increase in the size of the government debt. If we did not have to pay the interest on the debt that had been run up by his government and previous Liberal governments, we would not have had a deficit today.
Hear, hear!

Let me put that in perspective and context for the hon. member. When we came into office, there was a deficit in program spending in relation to the revenues of the government. We have now turned that into a surplus from a deficit of $22 billion to a surplus this year of $9 billion. We are paying our way in this government but we are still saddled with the debt that the previous government ran up and the hon. member knows it. I can tell from the smile on his face.
The Auditor General says you mismanaged the country.

If the hon. member wants to look at specific quotes that the Auditor General has made, he will read where the Auditor General says that we have great control of spending in this country. It is there in black and white in the report.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance, who claims he can control spending. Some time ago, Canadians dicovered that the Government intended to budget $4.5 million of their money to promote the GST. Now we find that this misleading advertising will cost not $4.5 million but as much as $9.1 million. Why should Canadian taxpayers have to pay for misleading Tory advertising?

Mr. Speaker, there is an advertising budget and there is a budget that involves a number of things, primarily for brochures, for the printing of the technical paper, for the overview of the technical paper and, yes, those things do cost money.
I remind the hon. member that when the finance committee returned from its trip to New Zealand a year and a half ago one of the things that the committee recommended in its report-I do not have the precise words here. In fact, I do. If the government proceeds with the tax, the committee recommends that it establish a private sector advisory committee to develop practical rules for the new tax, and to publicize the details of the new tax and the relevant social policy transfers.
It is very important for Canadians to understand the nature of this tax. If the hon. member refers to the CBC-The Globe and Mail poll earlier this week, he would see that 60 per cent of Canadians said they did not have enough information about the tax. It is very important for us to get that information out so that people can draw their conclusions about the new tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
If the minister wants to talk about the public opinion poll, I can remind him that 80 per cent of Canadians do not want any part of his tax, nor the advertising, nor anything else that goes with it.
The headlines in the newspaper today state that "The KGB has now abolished its anti-dissent unit, its top police". At the same time, Canadians know that the Government of Canada has doubled its anti-dissent budget in promoting the goods and services tax.
October 27, 1989

When are we going to get some glasnost in Canada? When are we going to get a government that stops using taxpayers' dollars to manipulate public opinion?

Mr. Speaker, we have both glasnost and perestroika in this country. The whole budget-making process, the tax reform process, has been done in a very open way. We have held consultations now for two and a half years since the White Paper was put out on the sales tax proposal. We have had another paper since the April budget. We have a technical paper now dated August 8 of this year.
In a very real way, glasnost is demonstrated to the Canadian people. It is all in pursuit of perestroika which is restructuring, withdrawing a number of the elements of the economy that are holding back the private sector.
If you go back to the November 8 economic statement, we stated our intention to introduce a number of ways that we would improve the functioning of the economy. Thx reform was one, open trade was another, incentives for investment, privatization, deregulation of energy, of transportation and of financial services, making for a more flexible labour force. I would be happy to send over to the hon. member a copy of the November 8 economic statement.

Mr. Speaker, on May 23, our research office filed a request through the Access to Information Act and on September 12 the Minister of Finance responded by saying the government would spend $6.6 million on GST advertising. Yesterday in committee, finance department officials revealed that $9.1 million of taxpayers' money would be spent to sell the GST to a reluctant and angry Canadian population.
I ask the Minister of Finance, was that $6.6 million figure given to our research department through access to information on September 12 not entirely the truth?

Mr. Speaker, as normally happens with this type of question, some of the information is left out of the preamble. In the letter of September 12, it states: "All records have
Oral Questions
been reviewed up to and including August 8." That information was provided to Mr. Keith Reynolds of the NDP caucus research bureau and was absolutely accurate.

Mr. Speaker, what we see here is the government making a 40 per cent increase in its budgeting in less than two months. This is the second incident in a week where the minister has been shown to undermine the access to information process. He is telling us one thing and doing another.
How can Canadians believe the assurances that this minister has given them about the GST?

Mr. Speaker, I fundamentally reject that because we provided the information that was requested. We made it quite clear what the information was, and then in this past week we have updated that information in view of recent circumstances. Surely the hon. member must admit that that is very open government, in providing all the information the committee needed yesterday and asked for yesterday in a very open way.
I see sitting beside the hon. member the member for Nickel Belt. We have had all this fire and brimstone from the NDP members of Parliament about what a terrible thing the goods and services tax is, but then the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt says: "I would like to see a tax at the retail level of 5 per cent". So he is accepting the principle of a tax. All we are arguing about is the rate.

Mr. Speaker, the minister told us $6.6 million. It turned out to be $9.1 million.
What else has the minister got in his back pocket? What else is he not telling us? I think it is time that Canadians got the truth instead of being subjected to contemptible government advertising. Is this the Minister of Finance, or is he the minister of propaganda?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member can have it both ways. The finance committee of the House of Commons, on which were sitting representatives of both opposition parties, agreed on the recommendation that I read out.
It is the fifteenth report. It is dated in early 1988 and it says that we must publicize the details of the new tax.

October 27, 1989
Oral Questions
If we do not have money to publicize the details, what are we going to do it with-tom-toms? Are we just going to speak on little telephones or what?
Oh, oh!

You have to use information like this-reports, brochures, and other forms of publications-to ensure that Canadians understand the details of the proposals so that they can make up their minds about the proposals.
Some hon. members have referred to the CBC poll that said 80 per cent were against this tax; 60 per cent also said they did not have enough information on which they could make that judgment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade.
Yesterday his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, indicated that the problems in the Scotia Fundy region were ones of overcapacity in terms of harvesting and processing, while the problems in the Newfoundland fishery related to science, the environment and other factors. If you assume that the problems are different, it is logical to assume that the solutions will be different.
I would like to ask the Minister for International Trade if he could indicate to the House that there will be a measure of fairness, that the Government of Canada will not participate in any mug's game to put Newfoundland fishermen against Nova Scotia fisherman, and that the solutions which will be put in place hopefully in due course will provide equity both for Newfoundlanders as well as Nova Scotians.
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
TVade): Mr. Speaker, that is the easiest question I have ever had to answer in the House.
We are interested in the problems of Canadian fishermen. We understand that Newfoundland fishermen are Canadians as are Nova Scotia fishermen, Quebec fishermen, New Brunswick fishermen, P.E.I. fishermen, British Columbia fishermen. In fact wherever there is a Canadian fishing we are interested in the problems of that Canadian fishermen. Equity and fairness is certainly the hallmark.
With reference to the Scotia Fundy Shelf this is a matter that is being referred as well to the cabinet committee led by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The task force led by Mr. Hache has been looking at the situation there. We hope to deal with this problem and to be as helpful as we can and as soon as we can.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary questions is for the same minister. At this very hour the community of Louisburg in eastern Nova Scotia, with an unemployment rate of 22.9 per cent, is involved in a march of concern to demonstrate its dismay at the possible closure of its fish plant throwing 400 workers out of work.
I would like to ask the minister, on behalf of the Government of Canada, what assurances he and this national government will give those workers. Can he, will he guarantee their jobs and thereby ensure that this community saddled with high unemployment will have some degree of certainty as it looks to the future.

Mr. Speaker, the firm of National Sea Products, as it is known, has been having some difficulties as have other east coast Canadian fishing companies. They have had losses now for a number of quarters. The company does not believe that they can continue taking losses and they are going to have to take steps that will minimize their losses and put them back in a profitable position.
Now it is not just Louisburg. The company has a number of plants in my own district of St. John's West. It has a plant at Arnold's Cove, a plant at St. John's, a plant at Burgeo, Newfoundland, and other plants in Nova Scotia.
We have had no information from the company that it has decided to close any particular plant.
We are expecting that they will consult with us before they do take any such action so we can be ready to do all we can to assist the people who were working in any plant that they might decide that they had to close, either temporarily or whatever the decision might be. We have had no such information.
Therefore, I can only say to the people of Louisburg: "We hope that your plant is not going to be closed. We will do what we can to see that it continues to operate, and we will certainly do everything we can to assist
October 27, 1989

anyone who might be laid off as a result of the present resource situation in the east coast fishery".

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my bosom pal, the Minister for International Trade, fresh from his bull in the china shop romp across Europe, only to find that his colleague the minister of fisheries is stomping around on our own china shop over here, frothing at the mouth about "prosperous times" he says "prosperous times in the Atlantic fishery".
The minister, to his credit, tells the opposite story. He does it graphically, even earthily, but he says it and he is on target, I say to him.
But what I want to know is: Who speaks for the government on this fisheries issue in Atlantic Canada- the Minister for International Trade, which I hope is the case, or the minister of fisheries?
Maybe, if the Minister for International Trade would stay closer to home and mind the shop, he could contain the damage being done by the minister of fisheries in the Atlantic fishery.

Mr. Speaker, when any minister speaks on behalf of the government then that minister is speaking on behalf of the government. There isn't any way to divide the matter up. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is speaking on behalf of the government and I trust that I am as well, and we are in perfect harmony.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has rightly pointed out that the fishing industry on the east coast of Canada is far healthier than it was four or five years ago.
Some sectors of it are always healthy; some sectors are not. In the inshore fishery every year there will be part of the coast where the inshore fishermen get no fish, so that is certainly not healthy in that particular area. In another part of the shoreline there will be a very good fishery, so that fishery is healthy. The fishery can be both healthy and non-healthy, both at the same time. While the hon. gentleman opposite might not want to acknowledge that, that is the situation.
The minister of fisheries yesterday announced a new $28 million program for aerial surveillance and enforcement in the offshore, moneys that were never allocated
Oral Questions
or spent by the hon. gentlemen opposite when we had the misfortune to have them in government in this country.
Hear, hear!

You know, even when you squirm you're delightful.
Mr. Speaker, let us get this straight. The fishery is healthy and it is unhealthy; both versions are correct. The government believes both views, that the patient will live and the patient will die but even if it dies there is nothing wrong with it. Smack in the middle of all that glorified, beautiful bafflegab there is an admission from the minister who knows the situation well, that our fisheries is in crisis particularly in Newfoundland.
I ask him now: instead of dancing all over and trying to cover for his colleague who has admittedly embarrassed him on this issue, when is the government going to come forward with an adequate special and credible response program to address the needs of those thousands of people out there who are having difficulty putting bread and butter on the table?
Come to the rescue of your fellow Newfoundlanders, John, please.

Mr. Speaker, it was Oscar Wilde who said about Bernard Shaw that he had no enemies but that he was intentionally disliked by his friends. It could equally have been said about the hon. gentleman who is questioning me at the moment.
With respect to the question that he has asked, at the beginning of this year our fisheries scientists gave us advice that was startling different from the advice that they had been giving the minister of fisheries and the government in the previous five or six years in connection with the size and total allowable catches which might be made of northern cod.
As a result the government acted immediately. We appointed Dr. Leslie Harris, and I think several distinguished fisheries scientists knowledgeable of the fishery, to review the whole methodology and to recommend to the government what they think is the situation, what steps should be taken to ensure that we are getting accurate forecasts, and to advise us on what they think

October 27, 1989
Oral Questions
the TAC should be next year. Their report will be in by the end of the year.
The minister of fisheries has already allocated $3 million additional funds for research into the east coast fishery, what stocks are fished there.
Action has been taken. A cabinet committee has been appointed. A task force under a Mr. Stein has been appointed. There is action being taken every day, and we will have a plan in place to deal with the problems when we know exactly what are the nature and the extent of the problem.
Bread and butter, Johnny.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
A consultant's report which was mandated by the government of Manitoba and funded at least in part by the federal government says that the closure of the Churchill rocket range was a mistake, that its dismantling should be halted and reversed, that closing the range makes Canada dependent on other nations for its space program and is devastating to that program.
My question to the minister is simply this: Is the government prepared to respond to that report in a positive way and co-operate with the Manitoba government in reopening the Churchill rocket range?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows that report is being studied by the National Research Council which still has authority over that range. When it has had a chance to look at it, indeed it will make a recommendation to the government.

Mr. Speaker, that report says that the current Canadian rocket program with one launch every two years from foreign soil is inadequate to sustain scientific careers or attract young scientists.
This morning we have the manager of the Manitoba space program saying that the ideal situation would be for NASA or someone else to come in and reopen the base. The government of Manitoba has already found
that there is considerable demand for the use of that particular rocket range.
I ask the government: What position does it take with respect to the reopening of that range which it closed?

Mr. Speaker, when we have had a chance to review that report and when I have had a chance to review the report from the National Research Council, I will be delighted to make some response to the whole issue.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. Many of my constituents in Cariboo-Chilcotin, in fact many people across Canada, have been expressing sincere concern regarding the proposed legislation to ban the importation of semi-automatic weapons.
On behalf of law-abiding Canadians who possess legitimate semi-automatic weapons, I would ask the minister to clarify his intent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no intention of banning the importation of semi-automatic weapons, none whatsoever. The government is looking at the banning of further importation of firearms originally designed and manufactured to fire in an automatic mode which are converted to semi-automatics for importation purposes.
There is no intention at all to ban the importation of semi-automatics, only those originally designed and manufactured to fire in an automatic mode. Any such weapons that are currently in the country would be grandfathered.
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister responsible for Canada Post, I will direct my question to any other minister who is prepared to justify the substance of my question.

Oh, oh!
October 27, 1989

Oral Questions

On October 10, Canada Post informed communities north of my riding of Cochrane-Superior and of Keno-ra-Rainy River of a prohibitive, senseless 32 per cent increase in postal rates effective November 13, 1989. The first citizens of this country depend on Canada Post for their basic essentials.
In view of the fact that unemployment hovers around 50 per cent and 90 per cent in those remote areas, would the minister bring Canada Post to its senses and continue to offer a service affordable to the citizens of the north?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister responsible for Canada Post said in this House the other day that he was prepared and anxious to have a meeting between all those affected and Canada Post. That meeting is being arranged.

1.	Do Refugee Board members and adjudicators work together on the first level hearing and, if so, were training sessions offered separately for members and adjudicators?
2.	Within the Immigration Department (a) what person or persons conducted the training sessions for the adjudicators (b) what procedures were used to conduct these training sessions (c) what person or persons are responsible for updating adjudicators on changing world conditions as they affect refugee claimants at the first stage of the process?

October 27, 1989
Government Orders

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
1. The adjudicator and the Refugee Board member share, equally, responsibility for determining a person's eligibility to claim refugee status in Canada and for deciding whether there is a credible basis for the claim. As the presiding officer, the adjudicator may, from time to time, consult with the Refugee Board member on matters of a procedural nature, which have a direct bearing on the initial hearing into the refugee claim. Aside from the initial hearing into the eligibility and credible basis of a refugee claim, the adjudicator has sole jurisdiction over the conduct of immigration inquiries and the resultant decisions.
In preparation for the implementation of the new refugee determination system, intensive training sessions were held for adjudicators and Refugee Board members. While these training sessions were held independently of each other, many of the resource persons who participated addressed both groups.
2.(a) Training sessions for adjudicators were designed and delivered by a team of Immigration Adjudication Branch staff, made up of the Acting Senior Analysis and Procedures Officer of Adjudication Headquarters, two Section Heads; one from the Quebec/Atlantic Division and one from the Pacific/Westem Division and several adjudicators from the Toronto, Mississauga and Mirabel offices.
(b) Various techniques were employed in the delivery of training for adjudicators. These included lectures and presentations by resource persons and guest speakers representing various government and non-government agencies. The Legal Officer of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) addressed adjudicators on the definition of a Convention Refugee. They also received a presentation and attended workshops in a session on "The Refugee Experience" given by a Resettlement Counsellor from the UNHCR. A number of presentaions were also given by representatives of the Immigraiton and Refugee board (including the Chairman), the Department of Justice and by various experts and executive heads from within Employment and Immigration Canada itself. Mock hearings were conducted and audio-visual presentations were also made.
(c) The Immigration Adjudication Branch provides adjudicators with ongoing training, including a national training program provided on an annual basis, divisional training on an annual basis, monthly section meetings and any other training deemed appropriate. Adjudication libraries in every office contain an up-to-date index of inquiry and refugee-related jurisprudence and other documentation and material relative to the function of the adjudicator. The Immigration and Refugee Board also provides the Adjudication Branch with copies of papers profiling the current conditions in contries known to be sources of refugee claimants. These papers are distributed to all Adjudication offices across Canada.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-29, an act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other acts, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and Motions nos. 1,2,3 and 5 standing in the name of the Minister of State for Forestry.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising to speak on this bill. My riding of Surrey North is one of the ridings in British Columbia that was founded on the forestry industry. On the north it borders on the Fraser River which has been the highway for the processing of lumber and plywood since the turn of the century. The foreshores of the riding are still the main booming grounds along the Fraser River.
In addition, we have a number of very large mills in the north part of the riding on the Fraser River. These have
October 27, 1989

changed over the years. Initially they were big lumber mills and now they are mainly shake and cedar mills.
The population of my riding Surrey North, of course, is basically a working riding. We have a large population who live in the riding and work in the lumber industry, particularly in the lumber milling and in the plywood. Therefore, the economic health of the riding is very much dependent on the continued success of our forest industry and our lumber industry.
I want to go back and look at the record of the last two governments as it relates to the development of forestry in British Columbia and in all of Canada. In the 1984 election campaign, the Conservatives said that they would bring in legislation to create a ministry of forestry. It has taken them five years to act.
I think that is indicative of the government's understanding of the vital role of forestry in this country, that it is not profound because if it really looked at the economic value that the forestry plays in this country-in fact, it is one of the mainstream industries that keep this country viable-it would have acted on its promise immediately.
There seems to be a lot more rhetoric on that side than there is action. The government talks about trying to look at sustainable development, but even as late as this summer, 55 per cent of Canadians did not believe the government was doing an adequate job when it came to environmental protection and sustainable development.
I think the record of the Conservatives in the forest industry has not been very good, but it probably is one step better than that of the Liberals. The Liberals were even much more blunt about it as their leader said in 1984, while he was in Prince George, which is one of the heartlands of the forestry industry in British Columbia, that they were against a full department of forestry.
The decline in the forest industry over the last number of years is a reflection of the lack of inaction by the two previous governments. I think we have to consider what the forestry industry in fact means to the Canadian economy.
In 1986 the forest products exports were $17.9 billion. Lumber exports were $4.1 billion. Paper and paperboards were $7.5 billion. Other forest products were an additional $1.4 billion. In 1987 the total exports were over $20
Government Orders
billion. This compares with farm products of $1.4 billion, fisheries of $2 billion, energy exports of gas, $5.5 billion, and metals of $6.2 billion. The percentage of export industry that is dependent on forest products is very high. '
Fifteen per cent of all of our export trade merchandise in Canada is dependent upon the forest industry.
Canada supplies 23 per cent of the world's exports of pulp and paper and 23 per cent of the world's manufactured goods. When we are talking about our export market, we should realize we have let a lot of opportunities slip away on us because we have not developed the technologies and the industry around secondary manufacturing. The number of jobs that we sustain in Canada per unit of forest product harvested is not anywhere near what it is in many of other countries. I will talk about that again later.
In addition to the economic value forests have in this country, they of course are a very, very significant part of our ecology. They are the backbone that regulate and moderate temperature. They stop the erosion of soils. They are the habitat for our wildlife. They are part of our world-wide reputation for beauty and nature. Without them, of course, Canada would not only lose a tremendous amount of its economic wealth because of the export of lumber products, it would also lose a tremendous amount of its tourist trade which is dependent upon people coming to this country to see the exceptional beauty of our forests.
One of the things that disturbs me is that the funding for sustaining forestry has been eroding. This year $28 million less has been allocated than in the previous fiscal year. The Conservatives, while they are bringing in a ministry of forestry, are diversifying and confusing the funding for forestry. Instead of having the funding for forestry under the control of a minister of forestry, it is being chopped up all over the place. Some of it is going to the Western Diversification Fund, which means that the minister of forestry will have to go to another cabinet minister to get funds to provide the moneys that are necessary for reforestation. Furthermore, the number of reforestation projects that the provinces can undertake will be diminished.
British Columbia wants $300 million but the funds are not adequate and are not being granted under the Western Diversification Fund. The same thing is happening in the Atlantic region where instead of having it

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
under the ministry of forestry, it is in fact being put under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
Sometimes you begin to wonder if there is a real commitment to forestry to sustain development or whether the government is trying to play political and public relations games using titles like the Western Diversification Fund and the Atlantic Opportunities Agency.
I want to talk briefly about Clause 7(c) which is dealt with in this group of motions, enhancing public awareness of social, economic, environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests. I think we are all believe that this is mandatory. We are concerned that it not become propaganda for the Tory cabinet ministers, but that the government will develop unique programs that are community-based, which will enhance the understanding of the total community, so that we can have the type of forestry programs that are necessary for economic development and for the ecology.
In order to improve on that section, I would like to make an amendment to Clause 7(C). I move:
That Motion No. 5 be amended by adding following the word "forests" the words specifically concerning the value of sustainable development.
That clause would then read:
"(c) enhance public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests specifically concerning the value of sustainable development.
