Mr. Speaker, I just want to deal briefly with the amendment. I am a little bit concerned that when the definition of sustainability appears in this act that it talks in general terms about how development today will preserve our options for the future. That statement with reference to this particular section of the act is far too general.
It is easy to sustain trees. As some foresters tell us, it is like planting a vegetable garden. You can plant the trees, fertilize the trees, cultivate the trees, space and thin the
trees and in 70 years you are able to cut down the trees and start the process all over again.
That is what some people conceive as sustainable development in the forest industry. However, it sounds more like the practice of sustained yield that forest companies, foresters and people involved in the industry have talked about in the past. There is quite a difference between the principle of sustained yield, which we support here as well, and the principle of sustainable forestry. A forest is quite different from a collection of trees. A forest itself is a complex, living organism that is made up of trees, under-storey vegetation, insects and all sorts of animal life; its wildlife habitat, hydrologic resources, streams, waterflow, groundwater and microclimates and humidity. All of those things go to make up the forest as a complex organism itself which is quite a bit greater than the sum of its parts.
We are concerned that in the minister taking advantage of his powers under this section of the act that he is going to be talking strictly about the economic benefits of the forest industry and perhaps joining with some of the advertising programs that have been mounted by the forest companies, such as the "Forest Forever" type of programs which do not educate the public as to the problems that we have in preserving and sustaining our forests. My concern is that the minister be specifically empowered under this section of the legislation to talk about the specific concern of sustainability of our forests.
A few months ago the Brundtland report came down. Madam Brundtland and her committee suggested that something in the neighbourhood of 12 per cent of representative ecosystems be set aside in each country in the world in order to preserve a genetic pool that would be available in the event that we mismanaged our forests completely or we made errors in the way we managed forests. That has taken place in the past and continues to take place. The reason for Madam Brundtland's suggestion was that those areas of old growth forests be allowed to remain in order to repopulate the areas in which we made mistakes.
That is what I see as managing the forests in a sustainable way. It is quite different from managing trees according to the principle of sustained yield or sustained output. That is quite a different principle. We would like to make sure in this clause that the minister recognizes that as his responsibility from the point of view of

sustained yield, because we would all like to see our forest economy continue, and grow and thrive. We would also like to see our employment in the forest industry continue to grow and thrive.
I would like to see communities like mine, Port Albemi, Courtenay and Parksville on Vancouver Island, many of which are forestry based communities, or where people who work in the forest industry live and send their kids to school, continue to grow and thrive. They will do that if we manage our trees on a sustained yield basis.
Managing our forests is quite a different thing. It is absolutely obligatory on the part of this government and this minister in particular and the new ministry of which he will be in charge once this legislation is passed to also talk to the people of Canada and to emphasize to the provinces and to the people across this country the need to manage our forests, that complex organism I talked about before that is made up of trees, animals, hydrologic systems, climatic systems, wildlife habitat, and all of those things that are more than the sum of its parts. The minister has to talk about those as well and has to promote the continuation of those.
There is a problem in the management of our forest lands in this country today. As my colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway pointed out, there appears to be an inadequate process of environmental impact and assessment of forestry operations. There appears to be an inadequate public involvement process. As a result, the public does not feel that they as communities are adequately involved in forest land use decision-making. Other groups with equally important interests in forest management, those who manage wildlife, those who are involved in the tourist industry, those who have an interest in the forests as well, are not represented. As my colleague pointed out, the result of this has been land use conflicts ail across Canada that have grown to be very, very bitter conflicts.
He pointed out one that took place in Clayoquot Sound where it resolved down to the union having to go out and sue in small claims court to recover wages lost from environmentalists who, with the best of intentions, were using civil disobedience to block roads in order to prevent road building taking place which they felt was a threat to the forests in Clayoquot Sound on the west coast of my riding.
Government Orders
I do not question the intentions of either side. The problem was that there was no legitimate public involvement process in land use decision making. There was no legitimate environmental impact or social impact process which would have protected and optimized jobs in the forest industry, jobs in the tourist industry and other interests in forest land use.
In the absence of that process, what could those people do? They felt compelled, desperate and they went in and blocked roads. As a result, they ended up being forced to pay the wages of the loggers who had lost their jobs. I might add, the loggers were equally desperate, their jobs were being threatened by that action. It is hard to blame either the loggers or the environmentalists.
What is to blame in this situation is the fact that this government has not demanded environmental impact assessment procedures from provincial governments even though federal resources are affected.
The other issue involves the native interests in our forest lands. We see the same kind of conflicts taking place in Quebec. For example, the Barrier Lake Algon-quins were attacked by the Quebec riot police, with helicopters overhead. It was almost reminiscent of the situation in Afghanistan a few years ago. Those police, working on behalf and representing the interests of the government and the forest companies, refused any consultation with the Barrier Lake Algonquins. When they expressed their opposition in the only way that remained open to them through civil disobedience, the riot police were brought in. Their Chief was thrown in jail.
Today, as far as I am aware, absolutely no negotiation is taking place. In that case, the lands that are about to be logged are in a wilderness area, an area that was set aside to protect certain species of wildlife on behalf of both the native Indians of the area and the people of Quebec. Those things have been ignored by the Government of Quebec, and as a result native Indians have been thrown in jail. Those kind of conflicts are taking place all across this country.
Let us hope that government members will have had an opportunity to review the amendment, to give it some consideration and respond affirmatively to it because this amendment asks that the minister not only consider promoting the economic and the social benefits of our

Government Orders
forests and the forest industry but also considers sustaining the forest environment in our country which is quite a different thing from sustaining trees.
It is a good amendment. I am very pleased that my colleague moved it and I hope that the House will rise and support it.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this bill for the protection of our forests and, particularly, on this amendment, the first part of which originally came from the government to enhance public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests, and now with the addition made by my colleague, the specific direction of concern for sustainable development.
This has been a concern of Canadians for a great many years and not only for those who live in the ridings where there are great forests or where people depend on the forests for their livelihood, although that is obviously a very, very major concern for those ridings and for that reason a major concern for all Canada because it is such an important part of our economy.
However, this has been a concern from the very beginning of Canada. In fact, one of the first persons to warn about the possible loss of our forests before Canada was even extended to its present sea to sea extent was Sir
John A. Macdonald who said on June 22, 1871: "The sight of immense masses of timber passing my window every morning-", I suppose he was referring to the timber going down the Ottawa River "-constantly suggests to my mind the absolute necessity there is for looking into the future of this great trade. We are recklessly destroying the timber of Canada and there is scarcely the possibility of replacing it."
That was said 128 years ago by the first Prime Minister of this country. His warning does not seem to have been taken very seriously.
We are rapidly losing our forests as are many other countries in the world. We have been warned now that our forests are not just necessary to the economy, not just necessary for those who like hunting and fishing and camping or canoeing, but they are necessary for air.
We are warned about the dramatic losses of forest in places like the Amazon Valley, Indonesia and other areas not quite so dramatic, such as southern Chile where the Fascist government has sold off forest and mining rights so that the hills are absolutely denuded by strip mining and clear cutting.
We also find that the Soviet Union has now recognized that its forests are not unlimited and it is beginning to take thought for the preservation of them.
But in Canada it seems that in spite of Sir John A. Macdonald and others our forest industries are mainly allowed to be cut without adequate replacement and the government's replacement programs are not adequate.
In the riding I represent, the riding of Trinity-Spadina in Toronto, we do not have forests, certainly not forests for harvesting. We do have many trees and for that we have to thank homeowners of years ago and in our own time who planted trees on their private properties and the parks department that has a policy of trying to replace every tree with two trees. When one tree has to be cut down, the Toronto parks department in the city of Toronto attempts to plant two. That is good, but it is not nearly enough.
Just as one way of measuring it, it takes, so I understand, several healthy sized maple trees to replace in the air the oxygen consumed by one family automobile driven about 20,000 miles in a year. Now the exact figures can be refined one way or another but, in fact,
October 27, 1989

Government Orders
since we have a little more than one automobile per person in the city of Toronto, I believe we do not have enough trees to keep replacing the oxygen used by our automobiles. We depend on the rest of the country to supplement our oxygen. We depend on the forests of Canada to keep Toronto breathing.
As I said, we do not have forests in Toronto and we do not have many people directly dependent on the forest industry for a pay cheque. But my understanding is that every man, every woman and every child in Toronto from the moment of birth, wants to breathe and they want to breathe good air. It is becoming a problem in Toronto partly because of pollution from too many automobiles and partly because of so many heating plants. In most people's experience, the general temperature of Toronto has risen in recent years. There are just so many warm buildings in downtown Toronto.
Some people think we have too many people in Toronto. Some of the people came to Toronto because the trees in their neighbourhoods were all cut down. I lived from 1951 to 1954 in the Gatineau Valley where I was in charge of an Anglican parish. There practically all the white pine had been cut a generation or two before and people were then cutting the second and third growth for pulpwood. It is very difficult to keep the tree growth in balance with the pulpwood growth. When a tree gets to be four inches it is a salable pulpwood log.
Many of the people from the Gatineau Valley left the Gatineau, whether it was to go to Montreal or to Rouyn-Noranda or to Toronto because the saw logs, the lumber logs, were practically all gone and they could not all live off pulpwood cutting or such other small industries as there were in the valley.
So these people came to Toronto looking for work and they all expected to breathe. They have a right to breathe, and they have a right to work as well. But if we are going to destroy the forest they will not work and if we destroy enough of the forests they and we will not breathe.
It has come to the point where the scientists are warning us that we simply cannot continue to survive if we continue to destroy our forests.
This is the most serious concern I have and therefore I am very pleased that the govemmebnt has undertaken to do some enhancing of the public's understanding of this matter. I hope that solid educational material will be put forward and not glossy brochures bragging about how much the government has done.
It can put forward information, for example, on more specific matters. For example, 62 per cent of the sugar maples in Quebec have been damaged by acid rain. At current rates the Canadian maple syrup industry will be dead within a decade. Some of us enjoy maple syrup, Mr. Speaker. No doubt we can live without it and possibly we would be even more healthy without various forms of sugar. But it is a $40 million a year industry. What are those people going to do when the sugar maple trees are gone?
It was reported this spring in British Columbia that cedar, arbutus and Douglas fir trees in some areas were showing signs of damage due to acid precipitation. This morning the Minister of the Environment seemed to say that acid rain was not a problem on the west coast. I am not sure I caught his exact wording but if he does think it is not a problem, perhaps he should talk to some of the people in British Columbia who are concerned about the Douglas fir and these other trees.
I want now to take up a very important related matter which I hope the government will include when it is doing its enhancement program and when it is advertising the need for sustainable development. The forest and the so-called rural areas of Canada in many places are bound up with the sustainable development of our First Nations. In many parts of Canada the forest is an industry that has been operating for, I suppose, 11,000 years by the people who have lived there without destroying it. They gathered what there was from the trees or the rivers or by hunting wild game or sometimes doing agriculture in small clearings.
However, they did not destroy the forests. The forests were there for thousands of years until we Europeans came. I believe one of the ways of preserving the forests so that we in Ottawa, or Toronto or in the other cities in Canada can breathe-I hope the government will take this up seriously-is to grant the land rights that

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
Canada's First Nations are still demanding and of which they have never been lawfully deprived.
In eastern Quebec, for example, the Innu or Montag-nais people living around La Romaine are being harassed by the overflights by NATO. These overflights are bombing training for destroying the Soviet Union. In order to practise flying low under the radar they are destroying the way of life of about 9,000 or 10,000 Innu people in the land the Innu people call Ntasinan and that we call eastern Quebec and Labrador.
They are not only driving the Innu people out of their homeland, they are damaging the soil and the water with fuel pollution. They are damaging the trees, they are using parts of it as a bombing range, sometimes using dummy bombs, but soon if NATO goes in there they will be using live bombs. They are damaging the forests, disturbing the wildlife, polluting the rivers and turning it into a battle zone. This is the most extreme case in Canada. The government should be stopping this so as to protect Canada's forests in that area and the other areas.
There are Indian land rights which the Canadian Council of Churches are helping them to defend all across the northern parts of Canada. If this government is serious in the educating the Canadian public to the need for our forests in many different ways, they will include the need to protect Canada's First Nations in their responsible use of our forests.
There has not been very much education by this government or by any previous government on this matter of the land. Somehow or other the words of our first Prime Minister seem to be buried wherever he wrote them.
This amendment of the government to "enhance public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests" with the subamendment to include "sustainable economic development" is certainly a very necessary thing to do. It is much more important than spending $40 million trying to sell the trade deal with the United States or however many millions of dollars the government is still planning to spend selling the goods and services tax. It would be far more useful to acquaint Canadians in our cities and in our rural areas with the fact that we absolutely need our forests. Those who never want to walk in a forest or paddle a canoe down a river in our forest areas need our
forests because our cities will not survive without the oxygen produced by them and the other forests of the world.
This part of the bill I think is very commendable and I hope both the amendment and the subamendment will receive the support of this House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments about Motion No. 6 which is before the House, and the proposal that the bill should include in the minister's responsibilities the power to enhance public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canada's forests and specifically, according to the subamendment, to provide sustainable development.
I rise as a member from Saskatchewan, an area where I think it is generally not perceived in the rest of Canada as being a forested region. Yet the House should know that that riding of Mackenzie was virtually all forest originally and the forestry industry is still a very big part of the economic activity that goes on there.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, Saskatchewan is not all prairie. Only about a quarter of the total area is prairie and the rest is a mixture of open land and parkland. After that the topography is solid forest until you get into the Canadian shield. So for northeastern Saskatchewan, which is the area I represent, the farmers who are still there, though they are becoming fewer in number, arrived faced with the prospect of good timber and turning that timber into lumber for shipment out of the region for use in building towns and villages and farm buildings. This was very much a part of the early life of that particular part of the country.
All of us who still live there have parents or grandparents who were involved in the forest industry, particularly in the winter time. There are still two very large plants in the town of Hudson Bay which rely quite heavily on the forest industry, with a plywood plant and a stud mill that are both still operating at this time.
The reason that I wish to speak on this subamendment which refers to the need for sustainable development is just that. In this town with two large mills employing just over 1,000 people directly and indirectly, we have been told that the stud mill will have to close in June next year because the forests are being depleted of large enough timber within a transportable area. That, combined with
October 27, 1989

the agreement to impose an export tax on the product from that mill, as part of the negotiations that led up to the trade agreement, leaves us in the forestry business worse off than we were before. We had free trade in forestry products before the negotiations began. After the negotiations we had a tax on our own products before we could export them. As a result, the decision has been made that the mill will be closed and many of the people employed in that particular comer of the province will be looking for other ways of making a living.
We do have some other options. The stud mill was basically using spruce and pine. There are great stands of poplar which do not have much use, other than to produce local timber. Local people understand the value of poplar wood, but we have not convinced other users of the benefit of it. There have been numerous studies and projects launched to decide what to do with all this poplar. There is now a proposal going through the region, the location of which, by rumour, will be in either Nipawin or Hudson Bay, to utilize some of that standing poplar and aspen by applying a new technology to transform it into pulp and paper.
If it comes to pass, it will provide some of the employment that will be lost by the closure of this stud mill, thanks in part to the decision in the negotiations leading up to the trade agreement. Perhaps the region may be able to save some of its jobs and find another way of utilizing some of the trees that are in that substantially forested area. The total forest is shrinking somewhat because of incursions of farmland, but the area that has been designated to be forest is still there. It needs perhaps better management so that we do not have the boom and bust kind of harvesting, where a large logging and timber milling company will move in to utilize the resource, then disappear for the next 30 or 40 years. That has too often been the case in that region.
I think it is important that the new department of forestry take cognizance of the need for sustainable development, as the amendment that is before the House now suggests. As well, I believe that the new department, as a federal department, should use its powers to enhance public awareness of the social,
Government Orders
economic and environmental benefits to be derived from Canada's forests. I am not completely convinced that this new department will have very much power to do that. When I look at the powers that exist in the bill, as I read it, the new department will simply take over everything that fell through the cracks from existing agencies, boards and departments within the federal government.
We are all aware that most of the big economic decisions with regard to forestry tend to be made at the provincial level because the provinces have the jurisdiction over the production and harvesting of those forests within their own boundaries. Federal jurisdiction only applies when those products leave the provincial boundary. I suppose the main initiative for developing and establishing a department of forestry was probably pushed along most rapidly by the decision of the government in the last Parliament to establish the export tax on forest and lumber materials as they leave the country.
I think the industry had great difficulty finding a focus for their complaints to the government. Their thinking seems to have been that if there was a department of forestry, they would at least have had some place to focus their discontent. They were not happy with the results they obtained by dealing with the Ministers of the Environment, Agriculture, Trade and Commerce and any others who had a peripheral interest in the trade issue having to do with forestry and lumber products. So there was pressure to have a ministry of forestry and the Prime Minister was willing to expand his cabinet yet again.
The benefits that can accrue from this amendment are that the general public and presumably the provincial governments and the industry itself will be made aware of the benefits to be gained from participating in sustainable development. They will co-operate and provide the kind of regulation and management of our forests that will in fact have that result.
The resource that they are working with is extremely important to this country. Some of my colleagues have pointed out the importance of forestry and forests to the ecology and the environment of this country. As they have pointed out, more than half the total land area of Canada is covered in forests. In the 10 provinces alone, almost 80 per cent of the area is forested, approximately

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
four times the acreage that is used in agricultural land. As we drive through or fly over the country we cannot help but notice how large the harvesting process is. As we fly over British Columbia or northern Ontario, even parts of Saskatchewan, we see huge areas that have been laid waste as a result of the clear-cutting system we have in place. We can observe big bare spots on the landscape from one to five miles in the air.
Canadians have to be made aware of what that does when we clear huge areas like that. What happens to the local residents of small towns in the area when the resource that they are relying on for jobs is depleted? It is very difficult to continue strong economic and social units in those towns, to raise families, to establish churches and businesses, when the harvesting is done in such a way that forests are depleted and jobs are no longer sustainable.
I urge the House to support this subamendment and enhance the ability of the government to make people aware of how harmful that kind of development can be and how there are other options that we can adopt.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to support the amendment put forward by my colleague which adds to the motion of the minister to enhance public awareness of the social, economic and environmental benefits derived from Canadian forests, the further requirement or onus upon the new ministry to enhance public awareness of the principles of sustainable development regarding our forest resources.
I am also very pleased to do this within the context of the bill as a whole, which sets up for the first time, I believe, in Canada, a full minister and department of forests.
Before I get into the substance of my remarks, I would like again to congratulate the minister. I know he has had this goal for some time. It has been a long gestation period. We are finally getting there and what we are trying to do by working together, and I believe I speak for all parties in this regard, is to try at this time to set up a full ministry of forestry to ensure that it has the strongest mandate possible in order to preserve and enhance an industry that has both historically and in terms of its
economic contribution done more for Canada and Canadians than probably any other industry.
I am also very pleased to be addressing this particular amendment at this time because just last weekend in the city of Nelson, which is my home town, and one of the centres of my constituency of Kootenay West-Revelstoke, there was a conference called "Getting High on Nature". I think it will turn out to have played a very important part in increasing exactly this public awareness not only of the principles of sustainable development, but also the other mandates that are listed as being important functions of this ministry and department.
The conference "Getting High on Nature" was actually hosted by School District No. 7 which encompasses the city of Nelson and surrounding area. It was the brainchild of a Mr. Bob Harrigan who is a well known communicator, particularly in western Canada, on subjects related to the environment and more recently coupled with the phrase "sustainable development".
This conference included about 120 high school students and some 300 educators, both educational administrators and public school teachers from elementary and high schools throughout British Columbia and other provinces in western Canada. The key participants from across the country, some of them of international renown, dealt with a number of areas of environmental concern. I was able to be present at some of the ceremonial aspects of the conference between other responsibilities in the constituency and noted that regardless of which workshop-at least 20 or 30 workshops at which the educators and the students were working together to get a better grasp of the complexities of all of these issues-whether they were talking about soil, water or air, or any subject related to the environment, forestry always played a role.
There were, of course, particular workshops and a number of keynote speaks who dealt primarily with the principles of sustainable development and with the intricacies of the forest industry and its particular problems, but regardless of the single topic, forestry always played a part.
The minister will know, and anyone acquainted with the forest industry will know, that if you are talking about soil quality, a great deal of attention must be paid
October 27, 1989

to the impact of the forest cover on the build-up and maintenance of those soils.
When it comes to matters of irrigation and water tables, the preservation of a balanced forest is vital to that substance upon which our society depends for its very day-to-day existence. Of course in recent years, anyone with eyes to see and the ears to hear could not ignore the terrific impact that forest cover both in Canada and internationally plays upon the atmospheric environment, particularly in light of recent debates on the greenhouse effect and the dangers of global warming.
Of course many of the other discussions that took place at that conference dealt with the ongoing debate which is taking place between the various users of the forestry resource, whether they be loggers, fallers, sawmill workers, people in the plywood industry, hunters, naturalists, water users and other soil users. Everyone has a vested interest. The growing recognition by conferences such as the one held by Nelson last weekend or in the media generally in recent months, is that the principle of sustainable development means that those resources that we have always held to be renewable must in fact be made renewable. It is vitally important if we are to be able to derive a good living both individually and as a nation from that resource, or to be able to enjoy the recreational time that gives this nation and its people much of their own particular spirit.
Another event that happened within my own constituency recently I think also shows the importance of the coupling of environmental awareness and the economic importance of the forestry resource. The company which operates the pulp operation in Castlegar is now in partnership between certain Canadian economic interests and the Chinese government. The pulp mill in Castlegar recently announced a $630 million expansion program. It was interesting to note that in their public information release they suggested that one of the major reasons for that major investment at this time was the stricter and proper environmental standards that have now been imposed on the industry.
I particularly noted at the time that this release was giving strong credence to what many people have been
Government Orders
saying for years, that a new awareness and concentration on protecting the environment in fact can create jobs. Here you have $630 million being invested, a doubling of production in an area of the province of British Columbia which has the highest proportion of decadent wood of any other part of the province, causing the doubling of pulp capacity in an area in which that wood supply had to be utilized in order to make room for new forest regeneration. We were very happy not only because of the jobs that were being created but because the expansion of that operation allowed us to utilize our resource in a much better way, and, as it turns out, in a much more environmentally sensitive way at the same time.
I was also happy because it allowed me to use that as an example. All of us who are concerned with the economic well-being of those communities and the people dependent on this industry, and I have been one of them for the majority of my working life, can use it to show that we can have a resource that provides jobs, that provides strengthened communities and looks after our environment at the same time, as long as we do it intelligently and with a view to the needs of the future.
I have been involved over many, many years in a number of attempts through public meetings, the use of theatre music, to try to bring groups together, be they be environmentalists or loggers. We have attempted to bring them together in forums in which they can begin to meet on some common ground, and it is not always easy. Any other members who happen to come from constituencies that comprise strong representation both of woodworkers and those with a very strong feeling for the natural aspects of our environment, will realize that being a politician for those kinds of areas is not always the easiest thing to do. You are trying constantly to get them to find common ground, to continue to talk with each other in a reasonable manner and to respect each other's roles. But it can be done. Take, for example, two of my best friends, both who come from my own area. One is Jack Munro, president of IWA Canada. The other is Colleen McCrory, who is president of the Valhalla Wilderness Society and one of the chief, so-called, "hired guns" of the environmental movement in Canada. Many ministers here shudder when they hear her name because she seems to be able to get appointments and get things done in half an hour that other people would take months to do.
October 27, 1989

Government Orders
If those two people and the people who work with them can agree with each other on the needs and principles of sustainable development, working together to build a healthy forest industry and a healthy Canada for the future, then it is possible. I hope that the minister will accept this amendment and we can proceed together to build a stronger industry, a stronger Canada and a healthy environment.

Mr. Speaker, support of the sub-amendment which specifically supports the principle of sustainable development in relation to the forestry industry of this country.
I will begin first of all by saying one never knows how much one appreciates anything until one has lost it. You would understand that if you came from the Nickel Belt. Unfortunately, I never did have an opportunity to appreciate the luxurious growth which did exist in the Sudbury Basin before the Chicago fire and before the development of smelting nickel. The folks who had lived there for a long time told me of the lush growth on the hills, the streams which ran through the hills, valleys, the streams filled with trout. One old gentleman told me that when he was a boy he would go with his father and fish for trout to bring home for supper, and he had just gone about a mile from where he lived in the small community of Coniston.
If you have been to the Sudbury Basin in the last 15 years, Mr. Speaker, you will know what I mean because we have lost our forests. We lost them because we were greedy-I am talking about the species-and cut down the trees. Everybody attributes that to the Chicago fire because the wood from the trees cut in the Sudbury Basin really went to rebuild Chicago after the Chicago fire. Then along came the smelting of nickel which was done on roaster beds. They would cut the logs down and pile them all up into a huge beds, then they would put eaves on the ends of these piles and then light a fire. The ore would smelt and the nickel would run off into the eaves and be collected.
As a result of that, the SO2 finished off what little growth there was close to the ground. Once the growth was gone the wind removed the soil from the hills so that all we had was simply hills of bedrock.
We miss those forests. I think it really does detract from the quality of life. I know when people talk about the quality of life today we talk about food, the clothing we wear, the kind of houses we live in and the kind of cars we drive. But I think quality of life also speaks to the question of the environment as well because I think there is something very soothing about the forests. It certainly keeps man closer in touch with nature. So, we are attempting now to rebuild the forests. When I began my speech I said that in fact we do not know what it is like. We do not know what we have lost until we have actually lost it. We do not have it, and we want to rebuild it.
Today Canadians, as a nation, are much more aware of the importance of the forests in our country. I get letters from student groups in high schools who are pleading for me to intervene with the ambassador from Brazil, to write letters imploring him to cease the development in the Amazon Basin so that we can maintain the tropical rain forests. There is a heightened consciousness of the need to protect the forests, not only in the world but also in Canada. It is important to know in Canada, in particular, the importance of forestry to our country. Half of the total land area of Canada, 79 per cent of the area within the 10 provinces, is forested. Sixty percent of forest land is productive. Production of forest products in 1987 accounted for $38 billion. Only the food and beverage industry exceeded the forest industry's contribution to manufacturing in Canada.
In 1986 forest product exports were $17.9 billion; lumber exports were $4.1 billion; paper and paperboard, $7.5 billion; and other forest products accounted for $1.4 billion. In 1987 exports were up to $20.9 billion.
They provided Canada with a net balance of trade of $18.3 billion in 1987. Farm products in comparison accounted for $1.4 billion; fishery products, $2 billion; energy products including petroleum, natural gas, and electricity, $5.5 billion; metal ores and non-ferrous metals, $6.2 billion.
The forest product industries in this country account for 15 per cent of Canada's total merchandise trade. Canada supplies 23 per cent of the world's exports of pulp and paper, and 23 per cent of total exports of manufactured forest products. There are 840,000 persons employed directly or indirectly in the forestry industry, representing 7.4 per cent of all working Cana-

dians. The forestry industry provides the economic base for more than 300 single-industry communities across Canada.
Apart from that economic contribution, I think it is important to recognize that forests have a direct impact on the weather, something I think we have ignored in the past. The forests regulate the stream flow. I mentioned what happened in our area. Once the forest disappeared, the streams disappeared. Forests minimize soil erosion. I described what happened in our own area. It protects fish and wildlife habitat, and, of course, improves air quality.
Rain forests, together with oceanic plankton, account for 90 per cent of the world's photosynthetic oxygen. Yet I am absolutely amazed of how we waste our forests. Foresters who work in the bush in northern Ontario tell me I would be amazed at the waste in the bush, the slashing of trees and logs left that could not be hauled out.
You can go through parks just north of my riding where there was inappropriate husbandry of the forest. It was slash and run. There was no reforestation. Provincial governments entered into cosy deals with forestry companies. That was the whole reason for the countervail by the Americans on softwood lumber. The stumpage fees were not high enough, they charged. It was notorious in the province of Ontario that the stumpage fees charged were not sufficient to reforest what was being cut by the private sector. There was absolutely no consideration of the harm being done to the environment.
I want to say to the minister that I am personally pleased that we are finally going to have a department of forestry, promised in 1984, delivered in 1989. The Liberals would not touch it, of course. After 20 years of Liberal rule, the Liberal governments did not even recognize the importance of having a ministry of forestry. We have a ministry of fisheries and a ministry of energy and mines. But here is the most important resource to the economic well-being of this country as well as its aesthetic well-being and yet it had no ministry. I want to say to the minister that we support this bill, we support this subamendment, we are pleased that we will have a ministry. I am sure the trees are happy. I want to tell the government that I am going out to hug a tree.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I say to my friend, not only are the trees happy, but if you listen, the wood is happy too. I say that to my good friend from Nickel Belt all in jest.
I support the bill wholeheartedly, without reservation. It is a good idea. The minister was there a minute ago. I am sure he is hanging on to every word I am saying while out there. It is a good idea, I say to him, because one in every ten jobs in Canada is generated by the forestry industry. That is a figure we have heard on a number of occasions in this House and so we should because I submit that part of the problem in terms of the lack of profile that forestry matters have had in government and in attracting the attention of decision-makers is that politicians of all political stripes have not cottoned onto or tuned into the marvellous impact for economic good that the forestry industry has in this country.
A few years ago when the Hon. John Roberts was the minister responsible for forestry, I had the good fortune to be his parliamentary secretary for a couple of years. In that capacity, I got to know some of the people in the forestry industry, right from British Columbia to Newfoundland. The forestry industry, of course, is extremely well served and the country is well served by the calibre of people who are involved in the industry, both in terms of the government bureaucracies federally and provincially and in terms of people who have chosen to invest in the industry and who work in the industry.
I do not want to delay the passage of this legislation. That is not my purpose in rising. It is just to get on the record one or two concerns that I have and then I want to give notice to whoever on the other side is piloting this legislation through the House that I shall be finished speaking in just a very few minutes. Oh, there is the minister. I say to him and his colleagues that it is my intention to get a couple of things on the record and then hopefully assist the administration in getting this good piece of legislation moving through the stages before we rise for the day.
I have the honour to represent a riding called Burin- St. George's. In the center of that riding geographically there is a bit of geography known locally as "Bay Despair". For the francophones among us, you would probably pronounce the it "Baie D'Espoir". It is a tribute to the Newfoundlanders who live there that they are able to take what is a foreign language term and put it into very translatable idiom, particularly given the local

October 27, 1989
Government Orders
situation where the unemployment rate is of the order of 80 per cent.
Why is unemployment that high in that particular area? That is the highest unemployment rate of any geographical pocket in Newfoundland and, indeed, just about the highest anywhere in Canada. The term "Baie D'Espoir" in French means Bay of Elope. The story behind it is that when some people were lost at sea they thought their number was up and then realized that they were up a long bay and hence, they called it Bay D'Espoir. For them, it was exactly a place of hope.
In Bay Despair, as we call it, why is it that the English corruption of the name so accurately reflects the reality in that particular area? The reason has to do with forestry. If you go back over many years, you will find that in Bay Despair on the south coast of Newfoundland, the communities of St. Alban's, St. Joseph's, St. Veronica's, Bay Despair, Milltown, Morrisville and to a degree Conne River, the 6,000 people in those communities came to rely over many years-going back around to the turn of the century and before and until the late 1950s, about 30 years ago-on forestry as a generator of economic activity and a source of employment.
In the later part of that period ending in about 1957 or 1958, these people used to actually harvest wood which was shipped from Bay Despair to England as pit props to prop up the underground mining facilities in Wales and southwest England. Of course, before that, they also used to cut logs which were boomed and taken by boat around into the paper mill at Corner Brook, quite a long voyage by water for those of you who know the geography and the distances involved.
Here is my point. The Bowater Company was the company harvesting the wood for both purposes, the local paper manufacturing purposes and the export of pit props. Once Bowater ceased its operation there, what did you have on your hands? You had literally hundreds of people, mainly men, who had skills in harvesting wood which were no longer marketable because there was no longer any need for harvesting wood. You had a whole generation of people who were quite skilled at harvesting wood, familiar with the technology of the day but had nowhere to market their skills. Those people over time went to Labrador, to other parts of Newfoundland or to
various parts of the Canadian mainland to find jobs where they could.
I come to the early 1980s. The government of the day, the great Liberal government of Mr. Trudeau of which I was pleased to be a supporter introduced a forestry economic stimulation program, FESP for short.
Festering?
I think the member is coming awake. I didn't quite get what he said but-
He's one of your colleagues.

No, it was not one of my colleagues. It was one of the rump group that sits up there. They are supporters of the government but reluctant supporters so they sit well up on the far end of the Chamber. We meet here every day at this time, and you should really drop in more often.
I want to conclude on the point I was making, because I would like to leave the minister some time to make his remarks, if that is his wish. I want him in particular, if he would, to consider addressing the issue I just introduced-the issue of the Forestry Economic Stimulation Program, the so-called FESP. I have just spent some minutes describing to the Chamber the situation in Bay D'Espoir, why the unemployment rate is high. In capsule, it is because many people there have forestry skills and nowhere to market them.
For a brief period in the early 1980s they were helped by this government through the special FESP program. They were able to engage in various activities-silviculture, thinning, various functions which were related to their forestry skills. It provided much needed employment, but equally to the point it gave an opportunity for us to regenerate our good forest stands in that particular part of the country.
I see my time is up. I make a plea to the minister to indicate to us whether he has given some thought to restoring that kind of a program for the sake of our forests and at the same time to creating some employment opportunities in that particular area as well as the St. George's area of my riding which also benefited from the FESP initiative.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes, in concluding the affairs of this bill before the House to re-establish the Department of Forestry, to express my gratitude and that of the government to all those who have contributed to the debate throughout the country, those who have appeared as witnesses before the legislative committee including the Canadian Institute of Forestry, forestry advisory councils and all the various agencies which have an important stake in our forests.
I also want to thank my colleagues and friends in the opposition parties who have approached this debate with a spirit of co-operation and enthusiasm, all of which reminds us of the fact that our forests are an ever-increasingly important component of life in Canada, critically important to our economy.
My colleagues have spoken, on second reading and again in support of the amendments before the House, of the regional importance of forestry and its importance to trade and to jobs. I do not wish to take time to reiterate all that.
We also talked about new dimensions that are be equated with our forests today-the environment, the ecology, and the concept of sustainable development which is so critically important particularly to forestry, not just because it is important to restructure and reconfigure the industry so that it can be less harmful to the environment through the discharge of chemicals and agents into the environment but to the management of the forests themselves, which as we all know now are perhaps the most critical element of our ecological

system. It is said that our forests are the lungs of the globe.
I would anticipate that the new Department of Forestry will not suffer the same fate as predicted by some, as did the mandate that was established back in 1960. Today we are looking at our forests in a much different light.
One of our poets said some time ago that of all of nature's scenes it is the woods where she reveals her deepest secrets and bestows her greatest blessings and riches. How true that is when we look at it in the context of this debate.
Even in Canada there are limits to what the forests can produce for us if we do not take proper care. We will, of course, never run out of trees in Canada. Even in my province where 60 per cent of the economy is dependent upon our forests, we only use less than 30 per cent of the land base for commercial conversion. The rest is perhaps not as accessible economically or is so-called scrub or weed variety. Nevertheless those forests too are critically important to the environment. We are facing some very critical problems and some tough decisions have to be made.
We are engaged in serious conflicts over the use of our land, the need to set aside for environmental purposes certain critical areas that are ecologically sensitive. Of course we are required to respond to new demands for industry.
In the past I can recall reading in Hansard the words of Right Hon. Prime Minister John George Diefenbaker who pointed out in 1960 that it was estimated that industry would double in its capacity and its shipments over the next 15 years. Conservative as the then Prime Minister was, he was even too conservative in making those predictions because we went much further than doubling the output of this important industry. Today we have data and evidence which would indicate that over the next 20 years the industry will double again. Already we are the world's largest shipper of construction lumber, and we are playing the most important role in trade in many of our forestry products.
We are adding 100 million new people to the world's population. All of them will lay a claim to the scarce resources and, of course, the potential for growth in the
Government Orders
forest products industry is increasing at exponential rates. I predict that the present estimates are conservative again and the industry will require more fibre every year if we are to retain the share of our world markets that we have carved out for ourselves and indeed realize the potential we have to enlarge our market share. The countries with which we compete in world markets have very much reached their potential for increased yield and growth in their forests, harvesting second, third and fourth generation forests and having shifted to much more intensive management than we had to in the past many, many decades ago.
It is predicted by our scientists that we can get up to three times the volume of fibre if we shift to more intensive management modes. Really what this bill is all about is helping our industry make this transition, helping our industry improve its market share but helping our industry reshape its attitude toward our forests to the point where important business decisions are made not in accordance with market opportunities or the availability of investment capital but in accordance with the fibre that is available.
That requires us, of course, to equate all of the various concerns and all the various aspects of forestry. It means we will have to shift to more intensive management of those forests we have allocated for commercial conversion. It means that we have to look at other aspects such as tourism which comes to mind.
Tourism is an ever-increasingly important industry in our province of British Columbia, the second largest industry and growing. Our forests are the backdrop of the tourism industry so we have to keep that in mind and manage our commercial forests in a way that they provide an asset to that important sector.
Likewise wildlife, the streams and fresh air have to be considered in all of these equations. There has to be a refocusing of our research efforts, a mobilization of the combined efforts of everyone that has a stake in our forests, indeed, every individual Canadian, because our forests are very much a part of our psyche. They are part of our nature.
When you travel and mention the word "Canada", it is immediately related to forests, to tall trees, to the prairies, and some of the other assets we have.

October 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
As my friends on both sides of the House have repeatedly pointed out, we have a custodial responsibility, not just to future generations of Canadians, but to those throughout the world. It has been said-and I said it in my earlier remarks during second reading-that over the last 10 years the area that was populated with trees has declined on a global scale from 25 per cent to just over 20 per cent. If we allow these trends to continue, our own children would experience a complete depletion of the world's forests. Without forests the planet cannot be sustained and certainly life on the plant could not be sustained.
We have a custodial responsibility to the rest of the world to manage those assets which we claim as ours, claiming sovereignty over an area which is the world's second largest with the assets that we have. We have one-fifth of the world's fresh water, which our forests help to cleanse and replenish.
In conclusion, I would just like to say once again, thank you for the co-operation that we have received and thank you to many of the stakeholders in the forest community throughout the country for allowing us to take this important initial step to redefine the role of the federal government and give me an opportunity to exercise the leadership that the Prime Minister has mandated me to exercise through our country to reaffirm the concept and the spirit of the idea of sustainable development to ensure that our forests are able to meet the needs of the present generation without compromise to the future.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE DRESS CODE
speechtext:
That this House express its support for the decision of the Commissioner of the RCMP to revise the Force's dress code to allow Canadian Officers of Sikh origin to wear turbans, to more fully reflect the multicultural reality of Canadian society.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise at this time to speak on this very important motion at a particularly significant time for the discussion of this question.
I want to just again read out the terms of the motion before the House. The motion reads:
That this House express its support for the decision of the Commissioner of the RCMP to revise the Force's dress code to allow Canadian Officers of Sikh origin to wear turbans, to more fully reflect the multicultural reality of Canadian society.
I want to emphazise that this motion in fact supports a decision that was made many, many months ago, some 18 months ago in fact, by the Commissioner of the RCMP, a decision which has not yet been implemented by the minister responsible, the Solicitor General.
I want to as well take this opportunity to emphasise the hard work of all of my colleagues on this issue and to single out in particular a number of those colleagues who, hopefully, will have an opportunity to participate in this debate and who have asked that their support be acknowledged. They include the member for Surrey North who in fact made a statement in this House some weeks ago urging the minister to act; my colleague, the member for Vancouver East, our spokesperson on multi-culturalism, who I am hoping will participate in the debate; my colleague from Kootenay West-Revelstoke; my colleague, the spokesperson on the ministry of the Solicitor General, the hon. member for Victoria; and many others. Indeed I speak, I say with confidence, on behalf of all of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party in supporting this very important motion.
Earlier today my colleague from Victoria questioned the Minister of Justice as to when he would finally move on this important issue. The Minister of Justice indicated that the Solicitor General was studying the issue, that he would be consulting and that there would be a decision in what he called the very near future. Last June the Solicitor General said that he was "in a consultation process with my caucus and everybody." In September he said he was "still consulting".
October 27, 1989

This minister has abdicated his responsibility and his leadership in this very important area. In fact, I would have to ask with whom is the minister consulting? We know that he is a part-time minister, that he is also responsible for agriculture and that he has political responsibilities in the Quebec area. How much longer must we wait before leadership is shown in this important area? Why is it that despite repeated requests by the Federation of Sikh Societies to meet with the Minister to discuss this important question, he has refused to meet with these representatives?
I have a letter dated June 19 which was sent by Mr. Mohinder Singh Gosal, the President of the Federation of Sikh Societies of Canada, urging that they be given an opportunity to meet with the minister to discuss this question. Despite repeated attempts, the minister has refused to do so.
Who is the minister listening to? With whom is he consulting? It seems, because of the delay, that perhaps he is listening to the voices of some of his colleagues in the Conservative caucus, what I would call the dinosaur wing of the Conservative caucus, certain Alberta members of Parliament; the member for Wild Rose and the member for Calgary Southwest, who have suggested that this very important recommendation by the Commissioner of the RCMP should not in fact be implemented.
I know that there is division, discontent and confusion on that side of the House, but today we have an opportunity to send out a very clear message as a Parliament to the people of Canada who are watching this debate, not just the Sikh community, but all Canadians, as to our view. Will it be the view of the member for Wild Rose and the member for Calgary Southwest? The member for Wildrose is quoted as saying that "in western Canada the RCMP mean a lot to us", and they do of course, "and the uniform does. I want to keep it as it is." She went on to say: "Something must be done if we are to keep it forever as it is now".
Let us look at the history of the RCMP uniform. The Northwest Mounted Police were founded in 1873. If we are to look at the traditions that the hon. member has spoken of, the tradition was a pillbox. Does the hon. member want to go back to the days of the pillbox? It was in 1900 that the stetson was brought in at the urging of prairie members of the RCMP because of concerns about the sun.
Private Members' Business
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, back in 1873 and 1900, there were not too many members of the RCMP who wore skirts, nylons and high heels, at least not on duty. The reality is that the RCMP has changed with the times.
I would have hoped that the minister responsible for multiculturalism might have drawn to the attention of the Solicitor General the fact that the changes have been made. Instead, the minister responsible for multiculturalism has been silent while some of his Conservative colleagues have been fanning the flames of hostility and intolerance. That is shameful.
I suggest that we have again an opportunity in this session this afternoon to speak out and voice our concern about this kind of attitude. It is an attitude which has unquestionably led to a rise in the incidence of violence, hatred, and intolerance directed at the Sikh community, particularly in Alberta, where those members are fanning these flames.
Another Conservative member of Parliament, the member for Calgary North, has said that the tabling of these petitions has given rise to unfortunate incidences of prejudice and racism in Calgary. Ron Chahal of Calgary, the president of the World Sikh Organization, has said the frequency of obscene gestures directed at Sikh motorists by other drivers has gone up. That is the kind of atmosphere which is being promoted, whether deliberately or otherwise, by the attitudes of the hon. members.
We have seen shameful badges which have the head of a Sikh in a turban and say "ban this". That kind of badge has no place in a civilized society, and certainly no place in Canada.
I have asked why the minister responsible for multiculturalism has been silent. Understandably, the Sikh community is raising concerns in a more general sense as well. They are asking if perhaps this is part of a more general lack of understanding and concern about issues affecting this proud community, a community which has contributed so much to our society.
For example, there are deep concerns about the way in which the Air-India disaster has been dealt with and the fact that we are still waiting for a comprehensive inquiry into that terrible disaster which resulted in the loss of 329 lives and which also resulted in the blackening of the reputation of an entire community by certain unforgivable actions of CSIS and others.

October 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
Why has this government and this minister not spoken out on the serious violations of human rights affecting the Sikh community in the Punjab and affecting Canadians of Sikh origin in the Punjab? Why has the Secretary of State for External Affairs been silent on that? Why no effort to improve the very difficult problems of immigration, for example, with an additional consulate in the Punjab? Why no grants to the community for over three years? Why no amendment to the Human Rights Act to include the provision for reasonable accommodation which is so important to make that a reality?
I suggest that instead of listening to the narrowminded and intolerant voices of the minister's Conservative colleagues from Calgary, he should be listening to the Commissioner of the RCMP. The Commissioner of the RCMP, when he was questioned in the justice committee earlier this year, strongly supported this change. He said that the face of Canada is changing and he felt that the RCMP, because it has always had representatives of the country it has served in its ranks, needed to attract people from visible minorities and aboriginal peoples.
We have much work to do in that regard. In fact, of the 14,843 members of the RCMP, 14,418 are Caucasian and only a little over 400 out of 14,843 are non-caucasian, including aboriginal peoples. That is a record which has to be changed. That was one of the reasons why the Commissioner of the RCMP made this important recommendation. The Commissioner of the RCMP went on to say that there are other more pragmatic reasons. He pointed out that when the Air India investigation led to certain questions there were only two members of the RCMP who even spoke Punjabi. Even for those practical reasons the RCMP must welcome into its ranks and encourage the hiring of Sikh Canadians.
The Commissioner says as well that we need members who can bridge the psychological gap that sometimes exists between new Canadians and police and how we view police in this country. We need to be able to help them with their problems, to carry out our investigations in an effective way and to deliver to them a police service to which they are entitled. He goes on to note that to deny Sikhs the right to wear turbans would in fact be in
breach both of the Canadian Charter or Rights and Freedoms and the bona fide occupational provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Why does the minister not listen to the Commissioner of the RCMP who has made this very important recommendation? Why did he not accept that recommendation some time ago, before the flames of intolerance could be fanned by a number of hon. members opposite?
I want to say a couple of words about the significance of the turban in the Sikh religion because some people say this is just a question of tradition. This is not a question of tradition, it is not a question of a particular cultural artefact. This is a fundamental article of faith, an essential element of the Sikh religious faith. Indeed, there are five articles of faith: the kes, the kanga, the kirpan, the kara and the kachha. Each of these is a fundamental article of faith.
One of my correspondents has written to me with some background. He says that the turban is known in the Punjabi language as the pag. He said if we study Punjabi culture and Sikh religion, the folk songs, the proverbs and the sayings, we see that the word "turban" is used as a synonym with the words "honour of a person". So a turban is not just a head cover or protection of the hair and head, it is also regarded as a fundamental part of the honour of the Sikh that he must guard at all times at any cost. In fact, removing the turban from a Sikh's head is seen as dishonouring him. It is a fundamental part of the religious tradition and surely we must recognize that and respect it.
Indeed, I care far more about what is inside the head of a member of the RCMP than what is on top of it. If I am in a situation in which I have to call upon the RCMP for assistance, I do not care if they have a turban on their head or a stetson or anything else. I want someone there who is sensitive and able to do the job, as members are in these circumstances.
We are talking of a turban, in the case of members of the RCMP, of a particular nature. In fact, the RCMP turban is made of navy blue cloth and it has a strip of yellow cloth which is wrapped around it. There is a metal brooch of the RCMP emblem similar to the pin worn in the standard uniform cap which is attached to the front of the turban. It is a dignified and appropriate way to accommodate this very important request.

I want to note as well that we would by no means be the only jurisdiction to take this very, very small step because, after all, that is what it really is. The United Kingdom, for some time, has allowed all members of the police force of Sikh origin to wear the turban. In fact, Mr. Speaker, when we talk about tradition there are not many traditions longer than the tradition of the London bobby. Yet London police of Sikh origin are permitted to wear the turban and it has not resulted in any difficulties whatever.
The Canadian Armed Forces have changed their regulations to allow a turban which, again, is an appropriate colour and design, to be worn by members of the Canadian Armed Forces. Similarly, the metropolitan Toronto police force and the Edmonton police force have incorporated this important tradition, have incorporated this important element of religious faith, because it is not just a tradition.
I am very pleased that we have a number of representatives of the Sikh community in the House today. As has been pointed out by representatives of that community, any baptized Sikh would not be able to join the RCMP if he is not allowed to wear the turban. Sikhs simply want an opportunity to serve their country, our country, in the best possible manner while their religious faith is being respected. That is what this is all about and that is why it is so important that we take this opportunity this afternoon to send out that message.

Parliament has an opportunity this Friday afternoon to send out a message of confidence in our country, a message that we celebrate the diversity of our country. I appeal to all members of the House this afternoon, those who might think of talking this motion out, to think twice, because those who would talk the motion out are going to have to explain, not just to Sikh Canadians, but to all Canadians why it is that they are not prepared to celebrate the diversity of this country and not prepared

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE DRESS CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Burnaby has presented the House with a question relating to proposed changes to the uniform of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The potential introduction of the turban as part of the red serge Mountie uniform has elicited a very strong reaction from many Canadians across the country, both for and against the idea.
Many of those who are arguing against change are adamant that their position is not reflective of a desire to exclude individuals of Sikh origin or, indeed, any member of a visible minority group from joining the force. Rather, they are interested in preserving the red serge uniform as a symbol of Canada's history and tradition.
The most common question being asked in western Canada is, why surrender our tradition for another tradition? It is common knowledge that the wearing of a turban in the Sikh society is based on tradition and custom and not on religious grounds. The obligatory tokens of the Sikh faith are the five Ks, the Kes, the Kara, the Kirpan, the Kanga and the Kachha. Whenever we read a newspaper or listen to a newscast these days, we hear more and more about our distinct society and the preservation of our Canadian culture. The unity of this country has even been challenged when reflecting cultural desires.
While Commissioner Inkster may have had good intentions, I think this proposal for change was for the worst possible reason. If you make an exception for one group of people, where do you stop? In order to come to a satisfactory resolution of this issue, I believe it is important to understand why some members of the

Private Members' Business
public are so concerned about possible changes to the red serge uniform. To do so, both the history of the force and of the uniform must be examined.
The idea of a mounted police force originated in response to a need to establish law and order in the northwest in advance of any settlement. The solution of Sir John A. Macdonald was the creation of a paramilitary police, trained for the warfare, with preliminary civilian responsibility. Its model was the Royal Irish Constabulary. Accordingly, in 1873, the Dominion Parliament passed legislation for the establishment of a mounted police force for the Northwest Territories to be known as the Northwest Mounted Police.
Three divisions of 50 men each were mobilized at Fort Garry, Manitoba, where training and organization took place during the winter of 1873. Recruitment proceeded and reached a strength of 1,000 by the year 1885.
Once established in the northwest, demands upon the force increased. Members supervised trading practices, provided some relief and medical services to the Indians and they carried out patrols throughout the area. In addition, the force had an economic and cultural impact on the west as many members, upon leaving the force, made the west their home.
Furthermore, by the start of the Klondike gold rush in 1896, the Northwest Mounted Police was already established in the Yukon. From the start, the force carried out almost all the administrative functions of government. Its members acted as land agents, magistrates, police and mail carriers. After the peak of the rush had subsided civil servants had relieved the force of many of its administrative duties. A few years later, the force was also to play a prominent role in opening up the Canadian Arctic frontier.
In 1905, the first contracts were negotiated for the force to act under the direction of the provincial authorities to enforce the criminal laws and local statutes. The force was active in the campaign of the Canadian government to attract settlers to the prairies. By 1914, over a million settlers had arrived. The police became land agents, agriculture experts, welfare officials and immigration officers. By this time, the mounted police had achieved an international reputation for its part in bringing about the orderly development of western
Canada. It is noteworthy to add that the force sent contingents to fight in both World Wars.
In 1920, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, as it had become in 1904, absorbed the Dominion Police which had been responsible for federal policing in eastern Canada. In keeping with its national role, it was renamed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I have provided only the briefest of overviews of the origins and the history of the force. My intent was simply to illustrate why many Canadians identify with and are protective of the red serge uniform. In fact, the history of the uniform is central to this discussion. In keeping with the para-military role of the force, many of the traditions established in the early days were of military origin. These military traditions were nowhere more apparent than in the style of the uniforms of the force which followed the patterns of the British Army.
In accordance with Sir John A. Macdonald's apparent desire to keep the uniforms of the new police force simple, a jacket made of heavy scarlet serge with a wool lining was issued as the tunic for all ranks; dark blue cavalry pattern overalls, black boots and a pillbox cap or white helmet completed the uniform.
By 1876 officers were pressing for a distinctive uniform in keeping with their social and military status as well as one that would distinguish them from members of other ranks. An elaborate full dress uniform and a simpler everyday uniform were authorized. Scarlet was used for tunics of all ranks, partly because it was the traditional British military colour and also to avoid confusion with the blue-clad U.S. army.
Although the scarlet tunic coupled with the stetson hat is generally reserved for ceremonial occasions, this uniform still represents the image that most Canadians have of the force. This image is continuously being reinforced and promoted both within Canada and abroad through the performances of the RCMP musical ride. Based on traditional cavalry drills, the ride provides audiences with a unique opportunity to experience an exciting part of Canada's past.
Today the RCMP truly has a presence from sea to sea, across all provinces and in the north. In eight of the ten provinces the force is under contract to enforce the Criminal Code and provincial laws. Under comparable arrangements, the force provides policing services to over 190 municipalities across Canada. The RCMP also

has exclusive police jurisdiction in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
It is also important to note that the symbolic importance of the red serge, or the "significant" uniform, is recognized in the current RCMP regulations of 1988. Pursuant to the regulations, the Commissioner of the RCMP can approve changes to all uniforms except to the significant uniform. Any changes to the red serge require ministerial approval.
Today's uniform depicts neutrality, impartiality, tradition, history and heritage. This uniform is a symbol of Canada and should only be changed to benefit the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as a whole and only to reflect safety and comfort.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to speak to this motion. I do not want to derogate from the motion itself because I find myself very favourably disposed to it.
I want to refer to the phrase "officers of Sikh origin". I do not think origin is really at issue here. What we are talking about is a faith and not origin. The reference to origin is perhaps a little unfortunate and slightly distracting. That aside, I also want to refer to the portion of the motion that refers to multiculturalism. It is my view that here multiculturalism is not just a reflection but it is a true manifestation of the community itself. It is a reality for us all that many of our fellow Canadians fervently and proudly subscribe to a faith wherein because of their devotion to God, the creator, they do not cut their hair or kes as it is called, and for reasons of tradition and good grooming, it is bound in a turban. I have, and perhaps we all have, friends and neighbours who are Sikh and they are an integral, real part of our Canadian culture.
My father was a Mountie. All of my growing up years were spent with a man who proudly wore the uniform of that day. I remember trying on his boots more than once, those big high boots and the big stetson hat, which did not fit me at all. I recall one day my father came home with a tuxedo and a small hand gun, a concealed weapon. That became the RCMP uniform for a day or a week in
Private Members' Business
terms of undercover work. The uniform has changed. It has changed to accommodate women most recently.
In Halifax, where I was bom after the last war, I saw many uniforms from the services, as well as the RCMP. Even though I was not alive during the last two wars, I know that men of the Sikh faith have served with distinction and valour in service to our Crown. They did that with or without battle dress, with or without helmet, even though the absence of a helmet might have put them at greater risk to their lives.
In my riding of Scarborough, in metropolitan Toronto, the Metropolitan Toronto Police will shortly have men of the Sikh faith proudly serving in the force. They will do that without cutting their hair, without removing the turban.
The Charter provisions in our Constitution speak for themselves. I do not want to spend a lot of time on that, but I feel it is likely that if the issue is pressed in the courts, if we are truly going to rely on our Charter, then the courts will find almost certainly that men of Sikh faith should not be barred from serving in the RCMP simply because of a uniform requirement.
I have children in my riding playing football, ball hockey, and they have their hair, their kes, properly done up as they play these sports. I am confident, and I think the whole country is-I like to think it is-that these children can grow up and be able to serve as Mounties just as proudly as my father did.
